description: Climate change is a global issue that requires special attention because its impacts affect various aspects of human life and trigger natural disasters. The impacts of climate change in Indonesia are quite complex, including changes in weather patterns, sea level rise, and global temperature increases, which pose serious threats to natural ecosystems and ecological balance. Therefore, efforts are needed to improve public understanding of mitigation and adaptation related to climate change in accordance with the 13th sustainable development goal (SDG-13), namely climate action. This study will try to build a solution based on the development of a climate change knowledge management system in Indonesia to improve public understanding of the impacts of climate change in a sustainable manner through the use of digital tools so that the community can process independently. Factor analysis is used to identify dominant factors in the implementation of a knowledge management system to support independent socialization, and regression analysis is used to develop a model that can represent the performance of increasing understanding of mitigation and adaptation at present and predict future implementation strategies. title: Data Supporting a Dose-Response Model for Weather-Induced Colour Change in Wood
description: This dataset contains the climatic, colourimetric, and model-development data used to establish and validate a dose-response framework for predicting weather-induced colour change in wood exposed to outdoor environments. Climatic variables include air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, relative humidity, and wind speed. In addition, the dataset contains engineered interaction terms between climatic variables, cumulative weather descriptors, calculated weather doses, and colour response parameters. Colour changes are reported in the CIE L a b* colour space and include source measurements, processed datasets used for model fitting, and universal response curves describing the evolution of lightness (L*), redness-greenness (a*), and yellowness-blueness (b*) as a function of accumulated weather dose. The dataset also includes prediction outputs and model evaluation metrics used during calibration and validation. The purpose of this dataset is to provide transparent access to the data underlying the development of the dose-response model and to facilitate reproducibility, independent validation, and future research on climate-driven weathering of wood and other bio-based materials. The deposition of these data responds to reviewer requests for public availability of the source data supporting the associated manuscript. title: Data and Code for "Becoming resident in a warming world: Food availability shapes seasonal partial migration"
description: Abstract In migrating wildlife, plasticity in migratory behaviour is an important trait for responding to seasonal environmental variation and coping with anthropogenic change. Although partial migrants with a high level of migratory plasticity seem to be more robust to rapid climate change than full migrants, we have limited knowledge about the mechanisms behind migratory responses to the environment in partial migrants. Using a dataset of 691 fall migration seasons from 339 GPS-tagged partially migrant red kites ( Milvus milvus ), we quantify how two key environmental factors, deviation from the average temperature and food availability, affect migratory behaviour. Warmer than average temperatures tended to delay fall migration among migrants. Within a sub-sample of territorial adults, a supplementary feeding experiment revealed that supplemented individuals delayed migration and showed considerably higher residence rates (68%) than controls (43%) while the temperature effect was difficult to estimate because only few of the food-supplemented birds migrated. These results provide experimental evidence that future positive temperature deviations may affect migratory decisions of partial migrants mainly via enhanced food availability. This plastic, food-dependent migration behaviour predicts future increases in the proportion of residents in partial migrant populations, as well as increased resident occurrence in areas with favourable food conditions. This repository holds the data and code to generate the output described in the publication Witczak et al. 2027 (DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2026.2371). To replicate the analyses presented in the paper, use the file "REKI_mig_departure_decisions.R", which includes the complete analysis and figures. This file reads in some prepared datasets that are stored in the 'data' folder and were prepared using the script 'dataprep'. The script "REKI_mig_departure_MS_numbers.r" summarizes the sample sizes presented in the text of the manuscript. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23412693

description: Data and code for "Climate change is decoupling fixed calendrical knowledge from the natural events it once predicted"   Jun Guo, Enze Song, Yi Liu, Lixiang Song, Xinyu Chang, Shengchu Zhang, Yang Xiao, Xinyi Liu, Yunhui Bai, Shuhui Yang, Xiaojiong Xu, Yongchuan Zhang, Hui Qin. Many Chinese agricultural proverbs tie a natural event (river thaw, last frost, first snow, insect emergence) to a fixed calendar date such as a solar term, a nine-day winter period or a lunar date. We call that date the **anchor**. The anchor does not move with climate but the event does, so the number of days between them measures whether a proverb still holds. The paper evaluates 805 such proverbs at Chinese weather stations for 1951–2024 and projects them to 2100 with five downscaled CMIP6 models.   The folder has two sub-folders:   | Folder | Content | Size | |---|---|---| | `dataset/` | Annotation layer of 20,606 proverbs, test units, station-year events, coupling results, projections, station and model inventories (14 data files + `LICENSE`) | 21.5 MB | | `code/` | Analysis and figure scripts, annotation protocol and validator, station list, map boundaries (19 files + `LICENSE`) | 17.9 MB |     ---   ## 1. Conventions used in all files   - **Dates** are day of year (DOY, 1 = 1 January). **Trends** are Theil–Sen slopes in days per decade. - **Offset** = event DOY − anchor DOY, wrapped into (−182, 183] days so that a winter anchor paired with an   autumn event does not produce a spurious offset of about ±365 days. - **Season of an event** follows from its proxy: upward temperature crossings, last frost and last snow are   *spring-side* events; downward crossings, first frost and first snow are *autumn-side* events. - **Warm-side offset W** = −offset for spring-side events and +offset for autumn-side events. W > 0 means the   event falls on the warm side of its anchor (spring event earlier, autumn event later than the anchor). - **Coupled**: a unit whose mean offset over a period lies within ±15 days of its anchor (about one solar-term   interval), i.e. the proverb holds at that station. Sensitivity columns use ±7.5 and ±30 days. - **Annual hit rate**: share of individual years in which the event fell within ±15 days of the anchor. - **Unit**: one proverb tested at one station in its province of circulation (`pid` × `sid`). - **Station ids** (`sid`) are GHCN-Daily ids (`CHM000` + 5-digit WMO number). - Missing values are empty cells (CSV) or `null` (JSON). Text fields are UTF-8; proverb texts, province names and   basin names are in Chinese (an English key for basins is given in section 2.8). - Frost and snow events end in 2019 (minimum-temperature reporting at many Chinese GHCN stations deteriorates   afterwards); temperature-crossing events run to 2024.   ---   ## 2. `dataset/` — file by file   ### 2.1 `pheno_annot_all.jsonl` — annotation layer (20,606 lines, 7.9 MB)   One JSON object per anchored entry of the Jicheng layer (*Zhongguo Yanyu Jicheng*, 26 provincial volumes), 4–80 characters long. 5,907 entries are testable assertions.   | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `id` | str | Entry id (`Y` prefix = Jicheng layer) | | `text` | str | Proverb text (simplified Chinese) | | `province` | str | Province of the volume (Chinese) | | `counties` | str | County-level circulation record where the volume gives one (empty for 6,421 entries) | | `source_volume` | str | Volume title, e.g. 中国谚语集成·宁夏卷 | | `printed_page` | int / null | Printed page number in the vo

title: Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
description: Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability . This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70 ) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming. title: Data for [Experimental Constraints on Ion Irradiation–Induced Remanent Magnetization in Extraterrestrial Samples]
description: Remanent magnetization (RM) in extraterrestrial materials preserves key information on Solar System processes. However, in samples from airless bodies affected by space weathering, the effects of plasma irradiation on magnetic properties and RM remain poorly constrained. Here we conducted hydrogen ion irradiation experiments with various energy (10, 20, and 30 keV) and fluences (1, 4.5, and 9 × 10 17 ions cm -2 ) on magnetic meteorites and magnetite to simulate space plasma exposure, combined with hysteresis, demagnetization, and anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) measurements. Our results reveal that intense irradiation can impart irradiation-induced remanent magnetization (IIRM) under weak ambient fields (<50 μT) without modification of bulk magnetic properties, whereas low-energy or low-fluence irradiation produces negligible effects. Comparison of IIRM with ARM suggests that implantation-driven internal stresses may perturb magnetic energy states and promote remanence acquisition. These findings provide a potential mechanism for magnetic recording in irradiated extraterrestrial materials and constrain their exposure environments. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23467420

title: Data from: The legacy of past climate warming: strong local adaptation in rear-edge populations
description: Improving forecasts of species’ responses to climate change has become a central challenge in ecology and evolution as species distributions are increasingly disrupted by ongoing climate warming. Insight into this challenge may be gained through a better understanding of evolutionary responses to past climate change. The rear edges of species’ distributions are typically relict populations persisting in former glacial refugia at warmer range limits. As such, they form natural laboratories to study the evolutionary outcomes of past climate warming. Three such outcomes have been proposed for rear-edge populations: maintenance of high diversity due to long-term persistence, strong genetic drift following habitat decline, and strong local adaptation allowing persistence despite environmental change. Empirical studies rarely explicitly test these alternate outcomes limiting our understanding of evolutionary responses to warming climates. We tested all three evolutionary outcomes at the rear edge of the North American herb Campanula americana , by assessing genetic variation in a genome-wide population genetic study, drift load as measure of fitness decline due to drift in a controlled crossing study, and local adaptation in a transplant study. Rear-edge populations exhibited reduced genetic diversity within populations and high differentiation among populations, typically interpreted as evidence of genetic drift, yet show limited drift load. Instead, these populations expressed strong local adaptation, thriving in rear-edge habitats that were unsuitably warm for populations in the expanded range. This indicates that warm-edge populations may persist under warming climates by gradually adapting, even in the face of genetic erosion. Our findings highlight the importance of explicitly testing for all evolutionary outcomes, and particularly going beyond measures of genetic variation, when inferring evolutionary history. More broadly, these findings identify rear-edge populations not as relics of decline, but as underappreciated models for studying successful adaptation under long-term climate change. The dated annexes assign MGA 64.14 billion of these settlements to July, leaving MGA 130.89 billion attributable to April–June. description: Climate change has a significant impact on communities worldwide, including in developing countries like Indonesia. The Sustainable Development Goals, specifically Goal 13, Climate Action, reflect this. This study examines how demographic factors influence community strategies for adapting to climate change and its mitigation in Indonesia. 2024 was the hottest year on record, with the global average temperature reaching 1.55°C above the pre-industrial era (1850–1900). For the first time, the global annual temperature increase exceeded the 1.5°C threshold set in the Paris Agreement in 2015. The last ten years (2015–2024) were the hottest in recorded history, demonstrating a consistent global warming trend. In Indonesia, 2024 was also the hottest year since observations began in 1981, with an average temperature of 27.5°C and an anomaly of 0.8°C compared to the 1991–2020 normal. Sea level rise, based on satellite data, shows an upward trend of 4.3±0.4 mm/year. This study provides new empirical evidence from Indonesia on the role of communities in shaping adaptation responses to climate change. The approach used is based on the concept of climate change knowledge management and the knowledge management system cycle, with exploratory factor analysis and regression analysis methods for model development. The results obtained are the existence of several new factors that can be used as indicators of success in strengthening community capacity and resilience in facing climate change now and in the future. Double boundary drift: geographical indication boundaries under climate change and administrative reorganisation - the case of Son La coffee, Vietnam
description: Geographical indications (GIs) link a product to its place of origin. Where that place is written as a list of administrative units, the legal description and the land it denotes can come apart. We conceptualise this as double boundary drift : institutional drift, when the units describing a GI area are renamed, amalgamated or abolished, and ecological drift, when land sustainably suited to the product shifts under climate change. We argue that administrative reform opens an amendment of the area that climate change alone rarely triggers, and that this amendment is the moment to re-anchor the boundary. We examine the Son La coffee GI (Vietnam), registered in 2017 as 24 communes, combining the 2025 commune amalgamation with an Arabica suitability model under five global climate models, two shared socioeconomic pathways and forest zoning. The amalgamation left 16 of the 24 names without a referent, and 10 of the 13 successor communes extend beyond the GI area. Only 61.5% (1067 km²) of the area is sustainably suitable, against 90.7% suitable. The gap is almost entirely protection and special-use forest, a misalignment present at registration, whereas modelled climate change lowers the grade of sustainable land (highest class from 16.4% to 4–5%). Institutional drift and ecological misalignment fall on different communes. Renaming would add about 785 km² without raising the sustainable share. Excluding protected forest raises the share to 90.3%; a hybrid boundary reaches 98.8% and keeps all producers but needs a digital map. Boundaries should be written in geographical criteria and reviewed periodically. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23435068

title: ECOLOGICAL DYNAMICS OF CRUSTACEAN ZOOPLANKTON AND THEIR CONTRIBUTION TO THE FOOD WEB OF TUDAKUL RESERVOIR
description: Crustacean zooplankton represents an important component of freshwater ecosystems and plays a significant role in the transfer of energy from primary producers to higher trophic levels. The present study considers the ecological characteristics of crustacean zooplankton inhabiting the Tudakul Reservoir, with particular attention to representatives of the classes Cladocera and Copepoda. The ecological importance of these organisms was assessed in relation to seasonal changes, environmental conditions, trophic interactions, and their contribution to the natural food resources of fish. Published data indicate that zooplankton communities of Uzbek reservoirs are composed of rotifers, cladocerans, and copepods, while Tudakul Reservoir has previously been reported to contain representatives of all three major groups. Crustacean zooplankton, particularly cladocerans and copepods, contributes substantially to the transfer of organic matter and energy within aquatic food webs. These organisms consume phytoplankton and particulate organic matter and, in turn, serve as food for fish and other aquatic consumers. The ecological significance of crustacean zooplankton in Tudakul Reservoir is therefore associated not only with its taxonomic diversity but also with its role in maintaining trophic interactions, supporting fish productivity, and responding to environmental changes. Monitoring the abundance and composition of Cladocera and Copepoda may provide useful information for evaluating the ecological condition and biological productivity of the reservoir. title: ELECTROCHEMICAL PROPERTIES AND APPLICATION  PROSPECTS OF ELECTROACTIVE COMPOSITE SUPERCAPACITORS BASED ON POLYANILINE
description: This article examines the operating principles of electrochemical energy storage devices—supercapacitors—and analyzes the physical limitations of conventional electrode materials. To overcome challenges such as large overall dimensions, low active surface density, and poor oxidation resistance in currently utilized supercapacitors, an approach employing polyaniline (PANI)-based electroactive composite materials is proposed. It is established that charge accumulation in the composite system proceeds via both the electric double layer (EDLC) mechanism and Faradaic reversible redox reactions. Conjugating the polyaniline matrix with an active substrate successfully eliminates the mechanical brittleness inherent to pure conducting polymers. Furthermore, the practical significance of symmetric supercapacitors for industrial power factor correction is demonstrated. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23336408

title: ENERGY SECURITY AND MACROECONOMIC STABILITY: THE ROLE OF SUPPLY RELIABILITY, AFFORDABILITY, AND DIVERSIFICATION IN CENTRAL ASIA
description: Energy security is usually treated as an energy-sector objective, yet its macroeconomic role in Central Asia, where five economies combine very different resource endowments and pricing regimes, is poorly documented. This article asks how supply reliability, energy affordability and diversification relate to macroeconomic stability in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, and through which mechanisms. Using a qualitative-comparative design, it synthesises ten peer-reviewed studies and several institutional reports located through scholarly search, compares the concentration of national power systems using 2026 Eurasian Development Bank figures, and examines four country cases. The evidence indicates that (i) unreliable supply imposes measurable real-economy costs, most visibly in hydropower-dependent Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan; (ii) affordability achieved through below-cost tariffs shifts costs onto public budgets, as Uzbekistan’s subsidy experience shows; and (iii) every country depends on a single source for 63–99% of its supply, which amplifies exposure to seasonal, price and import shocks. For the energy exporter, Kazakhstan, oil prices transmit to inflation through exchange rates. The article concludes that energy security supports macroeconomic stability chiefly when reliability and fiscally sustainable pricing are achieved together, and proposes a five-country panel design for formal testing. title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height : Surface elevation wnd100m : Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth : Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness : Surface roughness length influx_toa : Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo : Surface albedo temperature : Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature : Soil temperature at level 4 runoff : Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct : Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse : Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude : Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth : Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN . title: Enhancing energy delivery does not remove the acutely blocked but surviving margin: a unified biophysical analysis of radiofrequency, cryo and pulsed field ablation in myocardial walls of different thickness
description: Background. Acute electrical endpoints, pulmonary vein isolation, loss of local electrograms, non-inducibility, are achieved in almost every radiofrequency (RF), cryo and pulsed field ablation (PFA) procedure, yet conduction recovers in a substantial fraction of patients. Each modality has been enhanced to enlarge lesions: higher power and shorter duration, contact-force and dose indices for RF; second-generation and constant-pressure balloons, colder cryogens and tailored dosing for cryo; optimised waveforms, higher voltage, repeated applications and larger footprints for PFA. We asked whether these enhancements eliminate the tissue that is electrically silent at the end of the procedure but survives. Methods. Axisymmetric finite-volume models of a catheter or balloon on a myocardial slab 2–10 mm thick, with blood above and epicardial fat behind, were solved for 18 clinically representative settings, bipolar delivery between catheters on the two faces of the interventricular septum (6–15 mm, blood on both sides) was modelled separately, and a three-dimensional model of a circular multi-electrode bipolar catheter with real device electrode geometry was solved for seven further settings. RF was modelled with the Laplace and Pennes equations and Arrhenius damage; cryo with an enthalpy formulation including phase change; PFA with the Laplace equation and field-dependent conductivity, plus Joule heating. Tissue perfusion was present during energy delivery and absent afterwards. For each modality a lethal criterion (Arrhenius index Ω ≥ 1; minimum temperature ≤ −30 °C; field ≥ 636 V/cm, or 423 V/cm after repeated applications) and an acute-block criterion (Ω ≥ 0.1; tissue frozen; field ≥ 318 V/cm) defined the permanent lesion and the acutely blocked but surviving margin. Lesion lines were analysed through critical spacings for a lethal and for an acutely blocked midpoint. Results. Every setting produced a surviving margin. Its maximal lateral width was 0.8–2.9 mm for RF, 1.2–2.2 mm for cryo and 1.0–4.8 mm for PFA, and in 8-mm walls the surviving-to-lethal volume ratio ranged from 0.58 (repeated septal bipolar PFA) to 6.8 (double focal freeze). Enhancements that prolong or intensify the same field, longer RF duration, double or longer freezes, higher PFA voltage, larger footprint, deepened the lesion but widened the margin in absolute terms. Enhancements that concentrate dose, high-power short-duration RF and repeated PFA at a fixed outer field, narrowed the margin to 0.8–1.6 mm but did not remove it. In 3-mm walls, lines spaced more closely than a modality-specific critical spacing (3.8–6.8 mm for RF and ultra-low-temperature cryo; 7–20 mm for PFA) killed the midpoint, whereas a window of 1.6–8.0 mm beyond it produced midpoints that appeared blocked acutely but survived. In 8-mm walls no unipolar setting produced a transmural lethal line, and surviving but blocked tissue persisted at the midpoint for all settings. With catheters on both faces of the septum, the field between them produced a lethal zone at each face; septa up to 8 mm were transmurally lethal at 1000 V, but in thicker septa the zones were separated by an acutely blocked but surviving mid-septal layer (5.6 mm at 1000 V in a 12-mm septum; 6.6 mm at 1500 V and 1.8 mm at 2000 V in a 15-mm septum), and a lateral margin of 2.1–3.6 mm (1.0–1.8 mm with repeated applications) surrounded every septal lesion. With the circular bipolar catheter, lesions were shallower than with unipolar delivery and a 1.6–2.0-mm margin persisted across the line at all voltages (0.6–0.8 mm with repeated applications); in a 3-mm wall, 1000–1500 V left a 0.6–1.0-mm acutely blocked but surviving layer beneath the electrodes. Results were sensitive to lethal thresholds and to the tissue behind the wall but the margin persisted in all variants. Conclusions. Because energy field

title: Exchange in Transient Carboxylic Anhydrides
description: Data archive for "Exchange in Transient Carboxylic Anhydrides" The hydration of carbodiimides is commonly used to drive nonequilibrium chemical systems, often by converting carboxylic acids into transient aqueous anhydrides. This fuel reaction has found broad applicability in functional systems, from single-molecule motors to responsive bulk materials. The reaction cycle is usually presented in terms of activation (anhydride formation) and deactivation (hydrolysis) steps. Here, we investigate the additional role of exchange within the activated state. Slowly hydrolyzing anhydride dimers and polymers were generated using carbodiimide and then treated with distinct carboxylic acids. The formation of new anhydrides was monitored using 13 C NMR spectroscopy, allowing rate constants to be determined. The anhydrides exchange at an intermediate rate, with on the order of 10 exchange events per hydrolysis reaction under typical conditions. This process yields unique behavior. At long reaction times, the ratios of different anhydride assemblies do not trend toward the equilibrium distribution (fast exchange limit), nor are they determined solely by activation/deactivation rates (slow exchange limit). Instead, it is possible to favor distinct species because of the balance between exchange and deactivation. The implications of this result for the assembly of nonequilibrium species with transient covalent bonds is discussed.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23403819

title: Experimental Data and Carbon Footprint Assessment of Fly Ash Concrete Under Standard and Steam Curing
description: his dataset accompanies the research article entitled "Low-Carbon Precast Concrete: Quantifying the Ecological and Durability Restoration Capacity of Fly Ash Under Steam Curing." The study investigated the mechanical properties, transport-related characteristics, and estimated carbon footprints of concrete mixtures incorporating fly ash as a partial cement replacement under standard and accelerated steam curing conditions. Eight concrete mixtures were investigated, comprising two total binder contents (290 and 340 kg/m³) and four fly ash replacement levels (0%, 10%, 20%, and 30%), with a constant water-to-binder ratio of 0.50. The dataset includes: Compressive strength: 32 individual 28-day compressive-strength measurements, corresponding summary statistics, and reported 1-day strength values. Transport-related properties: Reported rapid chloride permeability test results, capillary water absorption coefficients, and maximum water penetration depths under pressure for standard- and steam-cured concrete. Mixture proportions: Cement, fly ash, aggregate, water, and superplasticizer contents. Environmental assessment: Estimated material-related carbon footprints, laboratory steam-curing energy consumption, strength-normalized carbon intensities, and sensitivity-analysis scenarios. Supporting documentation: A consolidated numerical results table and data-provenance information identifying the sources and interpretation of the reported measurements. Individual specimen-level observations are provided for 28-day compressive strength. The other experimental properties are presented as author-reported mixture-level results because complete, independently verifiable specimen-level measurements were not available for all tests. Consequently, uncertainty estimates are provided only where supported by the available experimental records. The environmental calculations constitute a screening-level carbon footprint assessment based on specified material emission factors and modelled curing-energy assumptions rather than directly measured electricity consumption. The dataset is intended to support the transparency, reproducibility of available analyses, and comparative evaluation of fly ash incorporation and steam curing in concrete production. title: FROM AQUEDUCTS TO SMART WATER NETWORKS: THE EVOLUTION OF HYDRAULIC ENGINEERING
description: Abstract: Water management is one of the oldest and most persistent engineering challenges. Societies have always needed to collect, transport, lift, store, and distribute water while controlling losses and adapting infrastructure to local terrain and climate. This paper examines the historical development of hydraulic engineering from ancient irrigation and gravity-fed water systems to mechanized pumping and contemporary smart water networks. Using a qualitative historical-comparative method, selected technologies are evaluated according to four criteria: source of hydraulic energy, method of flow control, infrastructure function, and relevance to modern water engineering. The analysis shows that the history of hydraulic engineering is characterized by a gradual shift from passive use of gravity and landscape toward active control through mechanical devices, pressurized systems, powered pumps, measurement, and digital monitoring. Ancient canals and aqueducts established principles of gradient control and durable infrastructure; Greek and Roman technologies advanced lifting and distribution; engineers of the Islamic Golden Age developed sophisticated pumps and water-raising machines; industrialization made large-scale pressurized supply possible; and modern systems increasingly combine sensors, data analytics, leak detection, and automated control. The study argues that contemporary smart water infrastructure should be viewed as the latest stage in a long engineering process aimed at increasing reliability, efficiency, controllability, and resilience in the movement of water. description: Climate gradients and habitat discontinuity structure genetic variation in a spring-specialist plant Dataset DOI: 10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdtj Description of the data and file structure We collected tissue from plants from 17 populations of crimson monkeyflower from the Southwestern United States. Samples for each of these populations were collected from distinct sampling sites represented by a large spring or seep.  These sampling sites are identified by unique two letter codes throughout this manuscript with exact location information recorded for all sites.   Crimson monkeyflower populations are limited to landscape features that support perennial water sources, such as mountain ranges and riparian corridors. Our populations were collected from eight geographically distinct landscape features, including two mountain ranges (Huachuca Mountains and Black Mountains) and six riparian corridors (Gila River, Aravaipa Creek, Verde River, Oak Creek, Colorado River and Virgin River). For each population, leaf tissue from four to ten individuals was sampled for genetic analysis. We obtained 19 additional tissue samples from herbarium specimens from unique sampling locations allowing us to sample the southern portion of the range, resulting in a total of 189 samples. Tissue collections consisted of 2-3 leaves, which we dried in paper envelopes using silica gel.  We ground tissue using a FastPrep-24 homogenizer (MP Biomedicals) and extracted DNA from samples using a modified CTAB protocol (Doyle and Doyle 1987) with quality control performed using nanodrop and gel electrophoresis. We digested genomic DNA samples using EcoRI and MspI before ligating to adapters and indices as part of a reduced representation protocol (ddRADseq; Peterson et al., 2012) . We performed size selection using a Pippin Prep (Sage Science, Beverly, Massachusetts, USA) to select fragments between 400 and 600 bp. Samples were then pooled into a single library and sequenced at the Genomics and Cell Characterization Core Facility at the University of Oregon using a single lane of an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, SP 100 cycle run. Alignment and Genotyping We demultiplexed sequences using fastq-multx (Aronesty 2013) and completed sequence assembly and genotype calling using ipyrad (Eaton and Overcast 2020) . Raw reads were quality filtered to allow a maximum of 5 low-quality bases per read (Q < 20) and require a minimum read length of 35 bp after adapter trimming. Adapter sequences were removed, and reads were mapped to the Mimulus verbenaceus genome (MvBLg_v2.0; LaFountain et al. 2022) using a clustering threshold of 85% similarity. Consensus base calls required a minimum depth of 6 reads (both for statistical and majority-rule calling), with clusters exceeding 10,000 reads excluded. The datatype for assembly was specified as ‘ddrad’ for this assembly, with two restriction overhangs specified (AATTC, CGG). Initial variant calling produced a dataset of 150,710 loci across 189 individuals. We used VCFtools to filter this dataset to remove non-biallelic loci. Loci were further filtered to remove those with a minor allele frequency (MAF) ≤ 0.02 and those with ≥ 60% missing data. After filtering out low quality loci, missing loci per individual were calculated and used to filter out individuals missing > 60% of their data, in order to avoid bias in downstream analyses. High levels of missing data per individual can bias downstream estimates of heterozygosity and population structure (O’Leary et al. 2018) . Lastly, loci were thinned to one SNP per tag to reduce linkage among markers. title: Food Availability in Brazil in Relation to Renewable Energy, Agricultural Land and Economic Growth – Research Data and Analysis Code
description: Description This repository provides the processed research data, Python analysis scripts, tabulated results, and supporting documentation associated with the manuscript Food Availability in Brazil in Relation to Renewable Energy, Agricultural Land and Economic Growth , submitted to Environment, Development and Sustainability . The dataset examines relationships among food availability, renewable energy, agricultural land use, economic growth, and urbanization in Brazil. The processed annual dataset covers 2001–2021 (21 observations), while the main first-difference analysis covers 2002–2021. Repository contents The deposited materials include: The annual master dataset in CSV format. Python scripts for descriptive statistics, regression verification, diagnostic analyses, and selected robustness assessments. Tabulated results, including correlations, descriptive statistics, model diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and data used to construct figures. Documentation of the computational environment, data provenance, and execution procedures. A README describing each file and instructions for reconstructing the analytical workflow. The underlying data were compiled from publicly available sources, including the World Bank, FAOSTAT, MapBiomas, and the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). Reproducibility and limitations The repository is a partial reproducibility archive. Certain statistical results were retained from previous calculations, and some original procedures, including the complete stationarity-testing workflow, underlying annual MapBiomas spatial proxies, and original Monte Carlo CUSUMSQ implementation, are not included. The repository supports verification of selected analyses and provides access to the processed data and available computational materials. It does not provide complete independent reproduction of every result reported in the associated manuscript. Individual files are documented in README_ZENODO.md. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23371244

description: This dataset was produced within the Horizon Europe project OptFor-EU – OPTimising FORest management decisions for a low-carbon, climate-resilient future in Europe (2023–2027). It contains outputs from forest ecosystem simulations performed with the 3D-CMCC-FEM model, aimed at assessing the impacts of alternative forest management practices (FMP) under present and future climate scenarios across Europe. Model description All simulations in this dataset were conducted using 3D-CMCC-FEM, a process-based forest ecosystem model that simulates eco-physiological and biogeochemical processes at daily resolution and hectare scale. The model explicitly represents species composition, age structure, stand density, and tree dimensions. It can simulates carbon and water cycles under different climate and forest management scenarios. 3D-CMCC-FEM has been widely applied across European forest ecosystems and constitutes a core modelling component of OptFor-EU (Collalti et al., 2014, 2018, 2024; Dalmonech et al., 2022). From the EURO-CORDEX generation CMIP5 downscaling experiments, high-resolution climate input data is available from the regional climate models (RCM) HIRHAM5-HADGEM2ES and RACMO22E-HADGEM2ES, for the Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 2.6, 4.5 and 8.5 (Jacob et al., 2020). title: G-IDSS - Dataset for a Decentralised Data Storage Service for Energy Communities
description: Measurement data, access control policies and analysis scripts for the paper "Decentralised Peer-to-Peer Data Management for Energy Communities". The deposit contains the results of eight experiments run on two clusters at the Technical University of Denmark, at community sizes from 2 to 1,600 peers: query scaling, the effect of the time budget under cluster and emulated residential networks, the saving from in-network aggregation over horizons of one day to one year, governance and consent decisions, an end-to-end trading cycle, community-scoped settlement with signed totals, behaviour with peers offline, and a comparison against a single store holding the same data. Also included are the data contract defining the community data model, the default and consent access policies, and the Python scripts that generate every figure and table in the paper. The data are synthetic: each peer holds quarter-hourly measurements for ten customers, generated locally from a seed derived from the peer identifier. Most runs use a thirty-day horizon from 1 September 2026; the aggregation experiment additionally sweeps one day and one year at fifty peers. No measurements from real households are included. See the accompanying software deposit for the implementation. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23479520

title: GIS-Based Dataset for Floating Photovoltaic Assessment of Hydropower Reservoirs in Türkiye
description: Description This dataset accompanies the research article entitled “GIS-Based Techno-Economic Assessment and Prioritization of Floating Photovoltaics on Hydropower Reservoirs in Türkiye: Energy Generation and Water Conservation.” The study presents a nationwide geographic information system (GIS)-based assessment of floating photovoltaic (FPV) deployment potential across 108 hydropower reservoirs in Türkiye. It integrates reservoir characteristics, spatial solar energy resources, evaporation estimates, techno-economic parameters, and multi-criteria decision-making to evaluate the potential contribution of FPV systems to renewable electricity generation and water conservation. The analysis considers four reservoir surface-coverage scenarios ranging from 5% to 20%. At 5% coverage, the estimated nationwide FPV capacity reaches 16.29 GWp, with an annual electricity generation potential of 25.76 TWh. Estimated annual water savings range from 71.34 to 144.48 hm³, depending on the floating system configuration. The techno-economic assessment incorporates investment and operating costs, levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), net present value (NPV), and electricity selling-price scenarios. Economic and infrastructure-scale screening identifies 51 candidate reservoirs, representing 4.24 GWp of FPV capacity and 6.84 TWh of annual electricity generation. Multi-criteria prioritization identifies Karakaya, Ilısu, and Ermenek among the leading candidates. The associated research materials are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further investigations into the integration of floating solar photovoltaics with existing hydropower infrastructure. Keywords: Floating photovoltaics; Hydropower reservoirs; Geographic information systems; Renewable energy; Water conservation; Techno-economic assessment; Türkiye. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23471460

title: GLOBAL SUCCESSES IN COMBATING CLIMATE CHANGE, PROTECTING BIODIVERSITY AND PUBLIC HEALTH.
description: This study examines the critical operational gap between macroscopic climate science and localized public health infrastructure through the implementation of the unified healthcare paradigm. Despite the abundance of ecological data at the macro level, translating these ideas into practical clinical interventions at the local level remains a persistent challenge. Using an integrated research project with mixed methods, designed for the period from 2020 to 2026, we are implementing a predictive machine learning system using random forests (RF) and gradient boosting machines (LightGBM). Worldwide, thanks to the implementation of this predictive architecture, an algorithmic accuracy of 88% in predicting boundaries has been achieved, which has given municipal medical facilities a 6‑day operational period for the proactive deployment of medical resources. The analytical work, combined with climate monitoring and medical management, provides a scalable empirical foundation for the global sustainability of the environment and health. title: GeoShift: a four-survey geochemical benchmark for cross-survey evaluation under detection-limit censoring (data)
description: GeoShift is a benchmark for evaluating machine-learning models across geochemical surveys under detection-limit censoring. This record archives its data. Observational arm: harmonised concentrations (mg/kg), left-censoring indicators and per-cell detection limits for 39 primary-core elements in NGSA (Australia, 1,315 samples) and NASGL (conterminous USA, 4,857 samples), with sample identifiers, coordinates, Köppen climate group and GLiM lithology for all 8,285 observational samples. GEMAS (Europe, 2,113 samples) is represented by identifiers, coordinates and fold assignments only; its values are not redistributed and are fetched from the Geological Survey Ireland publication on data.gov.ie by the code record. Controlled arm: Tellus (Ireland and Northern Ireland, 5,643 topsoil samples), with published X-ray fluorescence (XRFS) and aqua-regia ICP values for 47 elements measured by both routes, a left-censoring indicator per route, and limit provenance (38 elements accredited on both routes). Also included: frozen fold assignments (random, spatially blocked, environmentally blocked, leave-one-survey-out, pairwise and predictor-space protocols), element crosswalk, detection-limit tables, censoring audits and SHA-256 checksums. title: Ghana Climate Finance and Macrofiscal Context: OECD Commitments (2000-2024) with World Bank, IMF, Ghana Debt and GCF Records.
description: This dataset provides a curated compilation of Ghana’s climate-related development finance and macroeconomic context, designed to support research on financing instruments, creditor composition, concessional lending and sovereign debt. The climate-finance component contains 2,719 OECD recipient-perspective commitment records covering 2000–2024. A cleaned version excludes one flagged exact duplicate, leaving 2,718 records across the full period and 2,587 records within the principal analytical window of 2010–2024. Records retain provider names, financial instruments, flow classifications, climate objectives, activity descriptions, amounts and source references. The compilation also includes 19 World Development Indicators series, with coverage extending back to 1983 where available; IMF financing-arrangement history from a snapshot dated 31 August 2024; Ghana Ministry of Finance public-debt observations preserved by report vintage; selected Green Climate Fund project approvals, instruments and disbursement events; and a documentary register, pilot evidence notes and qualitative coding protocol. Selected project and documentary material extends beyond 2024 and is identified as contextual evidence. It includes the original research workbook, CSV snapshots of all 18 worksheets, eight derived data tables, a data dictionary, methodological documentation, source-specific rights statements and file checksums. A Python reproduction script regenerates the cleaned records, annual and subperiod summaries, provider-coverage tables, concentration measures and robustness comparisons without external dependencies. All eight derived CSV files reproduce byte for byte. Climate-finance amounts represent reported commitments rather than national receipts, expenditure or sovereign liabilities. Provider coverage and climate-attribution methods vary across years. Missing values are preserved, overlapping public-debt vintages remain separate, and regional project totals are not assigned wholly to Ghana. Documentary pilot findings are preliminary secondary interpretations rather than a completed qualitative analysis. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23269848

title: Global CO2 emissions from cement production
description: GCP-CEM: The Global Carbon Project CEMent-process emissions dataset This is an update of the dataset documented in: Andrew, R.M., 2019. Global CO2 emissions from cement production, 1928–2018. Earth System Science Data 11, 1675–1710. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-11-1675-2019 . Data in this release cover the period 1880–2025. title: Global livestock heat stress losses with endogenized adaptation feasibility (2000-2024): revised data and code (v5)
description: Revised data and code accompanying the manuscript Cost-effective adaptation can avert less than one-tenth of global livestock heat-stress losses (prepared for Nature Food, 2026). Contents: derived data for 2000-2024 at THI thresholds 68, 72, 75 and 78 (species-level gross, avoidable and residual losses, and value per head in 2005 constant USD); core model outputs and payback-horizon runs; a data dictionary; and the analysis scripts (loss model, adaptation/payback model, threshold-versus-linear bias, physical incompatibility area, and the US NASS reanalysis). The US NASS state-month panel (n = 3,144, 24 states, 2013-2025) supports a threshold response under a threshold-linear model with state, month and year fixed effects: breakpoint THI 66.2, post-threshold slope -14.8 lbs per cow per month per THI unit, delta-AIC = 49.4 (unconstrained two-segment sensitivity: THI 63.1, delta-AIC = 54.8). title: Global map of Local Climate Zones
description: A global 100 m spatial resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) map, derived from multiple earth observation datasets and expert LCZ class labels. The LCZ map is based on the LCZ typology (Stewart and Oke, 2012) that distinguish urban surfaces accounting for their typical combination of micro-scale land-covers and associated physical properties. The LCZ scheme is distinguished from other land use / land cover schemes by its focus on urban and rural landscape types, which can be described by any of the 17 classes in the LCZ scheme. Out of the 17 LCZ classes, 10 reflect the 'built' environment, and each LCZ type is associated with generic numerical descriptions of key urban canopy parameters critical to model atmospheric responses to urbanisation. In addition, since LCZs were originally designed as a new framework for urban heat island studies (Stewart and Oke, 2012), they also contain a limited set (7) of 'natural' land-cover classes that can be used as 'control' or 'natural reference' areas. As these seven natural classes in the LCZ scheme can not capture the heterogeneity of the world’s existing natural ecosystems, we advise users - if required - to combine the built LCZ classes with any other land-cover product that provides a wider range of natural land-cover classes. title: Global organic soil disturbance and greenhouse gas emissions, 2001 to 2024: model outputs
description: Organic soils, including peatlands, contain large amounts of organic matter and can release greenhouse gases when drained or burned. This dataset maps organic soil extent and disturbance and estimates the associated emissions for 2001 to 2024 at 30 meter resolution. The maps and tables can help users examine where modeled emissions are concentrated and compare the contributions of drainage and fire. The downloads below include: A global map showing organic soil cover as a percentage of each 1 km cell. Separate maps of average annual drainage and fire emissions for each reporting period, also at 1 km resolution. Country and global summary tables, plus detailed results by country, climate, land use, drainage, and fire category. The maps are GeoTIFFs that can be opened in GIS software. Emissions maps report metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per cell per year. Summary tables are supplied as CSV files, and the detailed results are available in both CSV and Parquet formats. Results cover five reporting periods: 2001 to 2005, 2006 to 2010, 2011 to 2015, 2016 to 2020, and 2021 to 2024. Emissions are annual averages within each period. The final period spans four years. The model builds on the organic soil probability estimates developed by Isik and Hengl (2026) . We apply probability thresholds that vary by climate domain to define organic soil extent, then combine this map with land use, drainage indicators, and burned area data to estimate disturbance and emissions. The same probability layer and thresholds are used for all five periods. Emissions are calculated primarily using Tier 1 methods and default factors from the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement. Please cite the Isik and Hengl source dataset separately when using the probability inputs. To request the 30 m model outputs as GeoTIFF tiles or a Zarr dataset, contact Erin Glen at the World Resources Institute's Land and Carbon Lab: erin.glen@wri.org . Open access downloads for these files are being prepared, subject to institutional approval. Links will be added here when ready. Results depend on the source maps and emission factors and do not replace national greenhouse gas inventories. Blank or missing results should not be interpreted as modeled zeros. See readme_data.md for units, file descriptions, and guidance on using the data. This dataset accompanies Mapping global organic soil disturbance and associated greenhouse gas emissions, 2001–2024 (in press), in Frontiers in Environmental Science . The link opens the article abstract page.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22137130

title: HYGIENIC ASSESSMENT OF THE COMPLEX EFFECT OF METEOROLOGICAL FACTORS ON THE HUMAN BODY
description: This article discusses the combined effects of meteorological factors on the human body and the main principles of their hygienic assessment. Air temperature, relative humidity, air movement, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation and sudden weather changes affect health not only separately but also in combination. The article reviews an integrated approach to meteorological assessment, measurement of microclimate indicators, thermoregulation mechanisms and meteotropic responses. Possible effects of adverse weather conditions on the cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems are described, together with preventive measures. Observation, instrumental measurement, analysis of health statistics and identification of risk groups are considered complementary methods in hygienic assessment. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23331488

description: This dataset provides high-resolution daily future climate projections for South Korea generated using the Hybrid Delta (HD) statistical downscaling method. The projections are based on a 16-member ensemble of CMIP6 General Circulation Models (GCMs) under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 emission scenarios. The HD method combines projected climate change signals from the CMIP6 ensemble with a long-term observation-based high-resolution reference dataset to preserve observed regional climate characteristics while representing future changes in mean climate and climate extremes.   The dataset contains daily climate projections at 1/16° (~6.25 km) spatial resolution for three future periods: 2011–2040 2041–2070 2071–2100 Daily projections from all 16 individual CMIP6 GCMs are provided for both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, allowing users to evaluate inter-model uncertainty or construct customized multi-model ensembles.   Data format Spatial resolution: 1/16° (~6.25 km) Temporal resolution: Daily File format: ASCII text File naming convention: data_latitude_longitude   Variables (column order) Precipitation Maximum Temperature Minimum Temperature Wind Speed   The dataset is intended for hydrological modeling, water resources assessment, climate extreme analysis, regional climate impact studies, and climate change adaptation research. title: High-resolution (100 m) daily temperature and relative humidity dataset for Belgium for 2020 from UrbNet
description: This dataset provides high-resolution (100 m) meteorological information covering Belgium for the year 2020, generated using the UrbNet machine-learning framework (Souverijns et al., 2026). It includes daily minimum, mean and maximum near-surface (2 m) air temperature and relative humidity. UrbNet is a convolutional neural network trained to reproduce high-resolution simulations from the UrbClim urban climate model. By combining large-scale meteorological forcing from ERA5 reanalysis with detailed land-surface characteristics, including land use, vegetation cover, building density and topography, UrbNet generates spatially consistent meteorological fields at 100 m resolution across regional and national domains. The dataset captures fine-scale spatial variations in meteorological conditions, including urban heat island effects, temperature differences between built-up and vegetated areas, coastal influences and topographic variations. It thereby provides substantially more spatial detail than conventional meteorological reanalysis products. Dataset characteristics Geographical coverage: Belgium Temporal coverage: 1 January – 31 December 2020 Spatial resolution: 100 m Temporal resolution: Daily Variables: Minimum, mean and maximum 2 m air temperature; Mean relative humidity Data source: UrbNet, driven by ERA5 meteorological forcing and high-resolution land-surface information This dataset is released as a sample of the UrbNet high-resolution meteorological product, demonstrating its potential for urban climate analysis, heat exposure and heat stress assessments, climate adaptation planning, and environmental research. Methodological reference Souverijns, N., Wouters, H., Veldeman, N., Francis, D., and Broeckx, J. (2026). title: High-resolution Multi-environmental-indicator Livestock Emissions of China (HMLE-China): A 1-km Stage-resolved Emission Inventory
description: HMLE-China v2.0 HMLE-China is a spatially explicit, stage-resolved, multi-pollutant livestock emission inventory for mainland China in 2022. The dataset covers five major livestock categories (beef cattle, dairy cows, swine, sheep/goats, and poultry), two production systems (extensive and intensive), and four emission-related production stages (enteric fermentation, housing management, manure management, and energy use). Version 2.0 contains 940 GeoTIFF layers organized into 28 ZIP archives , covering 10 livestock category–production system combinations, with 94 layers per combination. The archives comprise 23 ZIP files for extensive systems and five ZIP files for intensive systems. The larger extensive-system archives were divided into smaller parts to facilitate reliable uploading and downloading, without altering the underlying GeoTIFF data. The inventory characterizes greenhouse gas emissions, air pollutants, and nutrient-related emissions and losses across livestock production systems. Updates from v1.0: Forty-five redundant GeoTIFF entries were removed after verification that they duplicated existing extensive-system layers. Eight total CH₄ emission rasters were also corrected to address missing values arising during the aggregation of enteric and manure CH₄ emissions. The revised archive structure improves data accessibility while preserving the complete set of 940 unique GeoTIFF layers. The release includes file inventories, checksum information, documentation, and associated computational scripts. Detailed information on spatial grid properties, variable definitions, data processing, and version changes is provided in the accompanying README and CHANGELOG files. The exact geographic grid properties should be consulted when interpreting the nominal spatial resolution. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23369941

description: This archive includes supplementary file S6, used for a systematic review and Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis, studying the acute effects of meals matched for high or low protein content on adults' energy intake and appetite at the next meal. title: Historical Observations Data Platform Weather Stations
description: The Historical Data Platform (HDP) is a cloud-based, historical weather observations data platform focusing on near-real time to enable California’s energy sector access to high-quality, open climate and weather data in the formats that energy practitioners require. HDP applies best-in-class standards to historical weather observations to increase the number of reliable, accurate, long-standing observational records available to energy sector planners, including 8 variables identified as critical by energy industry engagement. HDP’s QA/QC pipeline included variable expansion (e.g., solar radiation, winds, precipitation) and careful handling for the kinds of extreme events facing western North America. The QC protocol is comprehensive, scientific, open, and transparent. Care was taken to address extreme events and ensure that the quality control process did not remove real extreme events while fixing issues such as sensor malfunctions. Inaccurate observations can cause serious problems for energy practitioners, leading to consequences such as incorrect maintenance decisions, missed safety thresholds, or over- or under-investment in grid hardening. This dataset supports ongoing efforts in electricity demand planning, asset placement, resiliency, and estimating renewable energy generation capacity needs, and serves as a critical localized dataset for future downscaling efforts of global climate models in the variables and resolution (hourly, sub 3km) needed in energy sector applications. The HDP dataset includes 15,064 standardized stations sourced from 27 open-access networks and covers 1980-2022, increasing the number of high-quality weather observing stations available to data users from ~500 to 15,000.   Dataset Format Note : Each station is stored as an independent .zarr in AWS S3 cloud storage. Open-access pathway to individual stations is provided in the  historical_wx_station.csv catalog. Please see the weather_station_data_access.ipynb Jupyter Notebook (Python) for access.    This dataset is included in California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment . title: Hotel Electricity Consumption Dataset for CNN-Based Forecasting and Gravitational Search Optimization (2023–2025)
description: This dataset contains electricity consumption records from a five-star hotel in Jakarta, Indonesia, enriched with calendar-related features to support electricity demand forecasting, energy consumption analysis, and cost optimization. The dataset consists of 910 daily observations collected between January 2023 and June 2025, where each record represents one day of electricity consumption. It was prepared to support the research entitled “Optimization of Hotel Electricity Energy Consumption Using Hybrid CNN and Gravitational Search Optimization to Support SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy.” The dataset includes electricity consumption during off-peak (LWBP) and peak (WBP) tariff periods, reactive energy measurements, and electricity consumption from three commercial tenant zones, anonymized as Zone A, Zone B, and Zone C. Dataset Attributes Each daily observation includes the following attributes: DATE: Date of electricity consumption record. DAY_OF_WEEK: Day of the week. IS_WEEKEND: Binary indicator identifying weekends. IS_HOLIDAY: Binary indicator identifying public holidays. WEEK_OF_MONTH: Week number within the month. MONTH: Month of the year (1–12). LWBP_USED: Electricity consumption during off-peak tariff periods. LWBP_PRICE: Electricity cost associated with off-peak consumption. WBP_USED: Electricity consumption during peak tariff periods. WBP_PRICE: Electricity cost associated with peak consumption. KVARH_USED: Reactive energy consumption. TOTAL_PRICE: Total recorded electricity cost. TOTAL_BUILDING_ELECTRICITY: Total building electricity consumption, used as the forecasting target. A_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone A. A_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone A. B_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone B. B_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone B. C_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone C. C_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone C. Research Applications This dataset supports: Daily electricity consumption forecasting using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). Temporal analysis of electricity demand based on calendar features and historical consumption. Electricity cost optimization using the Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSO). Analysis of electricity consumption under peak (WBP) and off-peak (LWBP) tariff structures. Evaluation of energy allocation strategies across building and commercial tenant zones. Research supporting Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7): Affordable and Clean Energy. In the associated study, a CNN model was developed using an input window of 14 consecutive days to predict daily building electricity consumption. The forecasting framework was combined with a Gravitational Search Algorithm to explore electricity allocation alternatives and potential cost savings under predefined operational boundaries. Data Confidentiality The hotel name and commercial tenant identities have been removed from the dataset. Commercial tenants are represented using anonymized identifiers (Zone A, Zone B, and Zone C). The dataset is shared for academic research purposes, subject to applicable data-sharing permissions. This dataset is intended for researchers working in energy forecasting, building energy management, machine learning, time-series analysis, and electricity cost optimization. title: Hourly dispatch model of the European 2050 power system under climate change: input data and results
description: Input data and model results for the article "Stress-Testing Europe's Planned 2050 Electricity System Under Climate Change: Price Impacts, Regional Vulnerability, and Transmission Constraints". The model simulates the European power system hour by hour for one year in 2050. Each of 30 countries (EU-27 plus Switzerland, Norway and the UK) is one node, connected to its neighbours by interconnectors. Generation, storage and interconnector capacities follow the ENTSO-E TYNDP 2050 National Trends scenario and are the same in every scenario. Electricity demand, solar and wind capacity factors, hydro inflows and thermal plant availability change with the climate. There are 10 scenarios: a baseline (weather year 2013) and three climate pathways (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP7.0), each with low, medium and high demand-side adaptation. Each scenario is solved as a single linear problem with linearized unit commitment in PyPSA. Files: - accreu_inputs.zip: everything the model needs to run (demand, capacity factors, hydro inflows, plant availability, capacities, costs, starting network). - accreu_results.zip: solved networks (PyPSA NetCDF), hourly prices, generation, curtailment and load shedding for each scenario, plus summary tables and the stress-event analysis. See README.md for a full description of the files. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23535332

title: Hourly hurricane wind fields for North Carolina: Florence (2018), Dorian (2019) and Isaias (2020)
description: Hourly fields of the 10 m wind speed and direction over North Carolina and the surrounding coast for three hurricanes that struck the state: Florence (2018), Dorian (2019) and Isaias (2020). They were produced for the Atlantic Marine Energy Center (AMEC) to estimate wind damage to power lines, and they give the wind at any site within the area of each storm, such as the location of a tower, pole or substation. The fields follow the blending approach of Wang and Bocchini (2025), with a parametric vortex near the storm center and the ERA5 reanalysis away from it. The record includes the three fields in HDF5 format, the IBTrACS best tracks, a comparison with 38 weather stations and a short description. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information (2026). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23399993

title: Hourly wind and solar generation profiles for U.S. EIA-860 plants (2020–2024) driven by TGW meteorology (1980–2024)
description: Dataset overview This dataset provides hourly capacity-factor time series for every wind and solar generator in the contiguous United States listed in the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) Form 860 surveys for 2020 through 2024. Generation is computed by running NREL’s reV  with  PySAM  ( windpower  and  pvwattsv5  modules) on plant inventories derived from EIA-860, with each generator forced by the IM3  Thermodynamic Global Warming (TGW)  downscaled climate dataset for weather years 1980 through 2024. For each EIA-860 plant year (the inventory of operating generators in a given vintage of EIA-860), 45 annual CSVs provide the hourly capacity factor of every generator under each historical weather year from 1980 to 2024. The data is intended to be aggregated at flexible scales — for example, to balancing authority (BA) level, or to nodes within a production cost model — supporting reliability assessments, long-horizon resource adequacy studies, and analyses of inter-annual variability, seasonality, and extreme weather events. title: HydroMap labels and protein structures for FastHydroMap
description: HydroMap simulation-derived residue labels for a frozen cohort of 1,000 protein chains, each with three independently seeded restrained explicit-water production replicas. title: Hygrothermal Aging Dataset and Performance of Thermoset Barrier Coatings for Infrastructure Longevity
description: Processed and derived data from an accelerated hygrothermal aging study of an epoxy barrier coating used for the rehabilitation of infrastructure. Coupons of a toughened epoxy composite were aged by dry-heat and by water immersion at four temperatures (20, 40, 60 and 80°C), for exposure periods ranging from an initial ~2-week sorption window to fourteen months of long-term gravimetric monitoring, and characterised by tensile testing (n = 5 specimens per condition), dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA; tan delta peak, ASTM D7028; n = 3 replicates) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; first heating scan; n = 3 replicates), together with gravimetric water-uptake measurements. This dataset contains the derived/processed results reported in the associated manuscript: tensile modulus, strength and elongation at break across four aging conditions — dry-heat aging for two months; water immersion for two months, tested wet; water immersion for two months followed by drying, to assess the reversibility of property loss; and water immersion for four months, tested wet — each reported across the four aging temperatures. Glass transition temperature (Tg) by DMA and DSC after two months of water exposure showed a comparatively narrow range (DMA ≈ 30–36°C; DSC ≈ 31–36°C) despite close to a two-order-of-magnitude change in tensile modulus over the same temperature range, indicating that Tg alone does not capture the extent of hygrothermal degradation in this system. Initial sorption rate constants at each temperature, together with an Arrhenius fit of the rate constant (apparent activation energy ≈ 10.1 kJ/mol, R² = 0.98, over 20–80°C), and the long-term (to fourteen months) 60°C weight-change curve are also included; the latter shows weight gain continuing for approximately eight months (peaking near 35%) before a subsequent decrease, consistent with a transition from diffusion-controlled moisture uptake to degradation-associated water transport (swelling, leaching, or partial network dissolution) at prolonged exposure. The raw, coupon-by-coupon water-uptake, mechanical and thermal data are openly available in DiVA and are not duplicated here; see Related works and References for the full set of underlying and related records. Background: I qualified at IRONMAN Barcelona 2019 in 10:02 h; the Hawaii slot was deferred to 2022 because of COVID-19. Achilles tendinopathy prevented run training for the six weeks before the race, and my plan was to run conservatively from the first step. Aged 58 in the M55-59 age group, I finished in 12:03 h (within the 48th percentile of age group M55-59). CORRECTION TO THE DESCRIPTION PUBLISHED WITH VERSION 1.0 The earlier description stated that a 2.5 km walking segment in the Energy Lab was planned, that the Energy Lab was the hottest section of the run course, and that running then continued to the finish line. Re-analysis of the GPS recording does not support these statements, and they are withdrawn. At a walking threshold of 2.0 m/s the marathon recording contains 17 walking bouts, not one. Four further bouts follow, at km 27.1, 34.4, 36.7 and 39.3. Because the recording contradicts the recollection on the turnaround, no claim about intent is made. The Energy Lab is the most radiatively exposed section of the run course, but it was not the section of the highest wet-bulb globe temperature. ASSOCIATED PUBLICATIONS 1. Population study, with R. title: Ice Anatomy: A Benchmark Dataset and Methodology for Automatic Ice Boundary Extraction from Radio-Echo Sounding Data
description: The measurement of ice thickness is of great importance for the accurate estimation of glacier volume and the delineation of their bedrock topography. In particular, this is a crucial factor in forecasting the future evolution of glaciers in the context of a changing climate. In order to derive the ice thickness, the travel time of electromagnetic waves in radargrams acquired by radio-echo sounding (RES) systems is analyzed. This can only be achieved by identifying the ice surface and underlying ice bottom in corresponding radargrams. Manually identifying these two reflection horizons in RES data is a laborious and time-consuming process. Consequently, scientists are attempting to automate this task through the use of techniques such as deep learning. Such automation can significantly reduce the time between a field campaign and the calculation of the glacier's ice thickness distribution. In this paper, we present the first benchmark dataset for delineating the ice surface and bottom boundaries in RES data, to facilitate straightforward comparisons of deep learning models in the future. The ``IceAnatomy'' dataset comprises radargrams and the corresponding manual picks, amounting to a total of over 45,000km of observations. The RES data originates from three sources: FAU, CReSIS, and AWI. The dataset comprises different RES systems as well as different pre-processing methods. In addition, the data was acquired over a large range of geographical and glaciological settings, featuring different thermal regimes present in Antarctica and the Southern Patagonian Icefield. This diversity ensures that the models' behaviors can be analyzed in different scenarios. We define a standardized train-test split for each source in the dataset. This allows us to introduce not only a baseline model trained on the entire training set (the ``omni'' model), but also three source-specific baseline models. The source-specific models are trained exclusively on the subset of the training data acquired by the specified source. The baseline models provide an initial benchmark against which subsequent models can be compared. The source-specific models demonstrate more accurate results than the omni model. For the FAU, CReSIS, and AWI test sets, the source-specific models achieve  Mean Meter Errors of 2.1m, 23.1m, and 4.9m for the ice surface and 9.1m, 78.2m, and 29.3m for the ice bottom. In relation to the mean measured ice thickness, these errors equate to 1.2%, 3.1%, and 0.3% for the ice surface and  4.9%, 10.4%, and 1.5% for the ice bottom.    For more information, please read the following paper: https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/19/5337/2025/ Please also cite this paper if you plan on using the dataset.   For the implementation of a baseline model please visit: https://github.com/ki7077/IceAnatomy   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23368993

The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right.
