title: Interaction between burial depth and N source in drip-fertigated maize: Agronomic performance and correlation with spectral indices.
description: Increasing drought severity and evaporative demand in Mediterranean areas makes it necessary to implement irrigation systems with high water and nutrient supply efficiency. The combined management of drip irrigation burial depth and different nitrogen (N) sources, thus far unexplored, predicting these effects using proximal and spectral vegetation indices. A 2-year field experiment was conducted comparing maize yield and N uptake from four N fertilization treatments: ammonium sulfate (AS), AS with the nitrification inhibitor DMPP (AS+INH), calcium nitrate (CN) and a control without N fertilization combined with surface or subsurface (30 cm depth) drip fertigation. Multispectral data were collected to calculate various vegetation indices, while the chlorophyll content was measured with a soil plant analysis development (SPAD) sensor in the second year. Subsurface drip and AS+INH increased maize grain yields compared to surface drip and AS-only (by 12 % and 18 %, respectively, P < 0.05). However, this was observed only in the second season, as were increases in grain N content. The  results show that the use of CN performed better in surface drip, while the use of NH4+-N-based fertilizers were recommended for subsurface irrigation. Regarding the spectral data, at the flowering-milky kernel and dent kernel phenological stages Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE) and the canopy chlorophyll content index (CCCI) were the two vegetation indices that best estimated agronomical parameters and were able to discriminate the phenological differences between irrigation systems. This study highlights the potential for (i) predicting yield and N uptake using proximal and multispectral sensors in drip-fertigated maize and (ii) optimizing crop performance by combining drip burial depth and N source (DMPP combined with subsurface irrigation), with relevant implications for climate change adaptation (i.e., potential improvements in crop phenology and water saving). title: Juno/JEDI grid-cell averaged auroral electron energy fluxes, PJ3 to PJ66, supporting "Hemispheric asymmetry and up/down anisotropy of Jupiter's auroral electron precipitation: Juno/JEDI statistics"
description: This dataset contains the processed data and the Python scripts supporting the figures and tables of Benmahi et al., "Hemispheric asymmetry and up/down anisotropy of Jupiter's auroral electron precipitation: Juno/JEDI statistics", submitted to JGR: Space Physics. The data are derived from the Juno/JEDI level-3 electron differential intensities archived in the NASA Planetary Data System (Mauk et al., 2026), for perijoves PJ3 to PJ66 and Juno planetocentric distances below 200000 km. Two corrections were applied before analysis, a power-law replacement of the small-pixel data below about 50 keV from PJ20 onward and the removal of the Minimum Ionizing Bump near 160 keV. The Juno magnetic footprint was computed with the JRM33 internal field model combined with the CON2020 current sheet model, at a reference altitude of 400 km. Footprints were sampled on a 0.33 deg x 0.33 deg grid in System III latitude and west longitude, and one average spectrum was computed in each grid cell crossed during each perijove. Each cell was assigned to the polar emission (PE), main emission (ME) or outer emission (OE) region using the Juno/UVS main emission masks of Groulard et al. (2024) and the mean Io magnetic footprint. Downward (planetward) and upward (anti-planetward) fluxes were obtained by averaging the directional intensity over the corresponding loss cone and multiplying by pi, then integrating between 30 keV and 1 MeV. Files jedi_gridcell_fluxes.dat gives, for each grid cell, perijove, hemisphere and flux direction, the energy flux in mW m-2, the mean electron energy in keV and the electron number flux in cm-2 s-1. It reproduces Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2. jedi_gridcell_spectra.dat gives the corresponding grid-cell averaged differential flux spectra, in the same row order, and jedi_energy_axis.dat gives their energy axis in keV. jedi_up_down_ratio_map.dat gives the ratio of the upward to downward energy flux per grid cell, all perijoves combined. It reproduces Figure 2 and Table 3. juno_footprint_tracks.dat gives the Juno magnetic footprint trajectories shown in Figure 2. auroral_boundaries.dat gives the mean ME boundaries and the mean Io footprint contour shown in Figure 2. auroral_boundaries_per_perijove.dat gives, for each perijove and hemisphere, the inner and outer ME boundaries used to assign the grid cells to the PE, ME and OE regions. They are the Juno/UVS masks of Groulard et al. (2024) up to PJ39, and the mean of the PJ1 to PJ39 masks from PJ40 onward. All .dat files are plain text, with header lines starting with # followed by one line of column names and space-separated values. They can be read in Python with pandas.read_csv(file, comment="#", sep=r"\s+"). The Python scripts used to read the processed data, assign the grid cells to the auroral sub-regions, compute the statistics and produce the figures are included, together with the script used to export these files. title: Kansas maize yield recovery under recurrent compound heat-drought events, 1981-2016
description: This dataset supports an observational spatial-panel analysis of maize yield responses and recovery following compound heat-drought events across 88 maize-growing grid cells in Kansas, United States, from 1981 to 2016. The deposit includes the processed climate and yield panel, compound-event indicators, event-onset and recovery-episode data, model outputs, sensitivity analyses, analysis code, data dictionaries, and quality-assurance documentation. Compound events were identified using cell-specific growing-season temperature and root-zone soil-moisture thresholds. The study evaluates immediate yield anomalies, multi-year recovery debt, repeated or persistent compound exposure, and robustness to alternative event definitions, detrending methods, covariance estimators, and percentile thresholds. Source datasets include GDHY maize yields, SAGE crop calendars, ERA5-Land temperature and soil moisture, and ERA5 precipitation. Users should consult the README and source-data documentation for variable definitions, provenance, and reuse conditions. Version 2 adds USDA NASS county-level total, irrigated, and non-irrigated maize yield and harvested-area records; the county-to-grid spatial crosswalk; irrigation-share construction files; yield-validation outputs; and irrigation-interaction and recovery-debt sensitivity results.   Version 3 (October 2026): This version adds supplementary data and code supporting the revised analysis of annual maize yield trajectories after compound heat–drought exposure. The addendum includes the archived USDA NASS corn-silking data and the reproduction workflow for Supplementary Table S11, the separate heat and drought severity analysis in Table S12, descriptive sensitivity results for the ±5% and ±10% two-season return criteria, and the data underlying Supplementary Figure S4. It also provides corrected return-time code that records the endpoint of the first qualifying pair of annual yield anomalies. This correction did not change the Cox model coefficients in the documented comparison. The original analytical packages and the Version 2 irrigation addendum are retained. The silking analysis is limited to years eligible under the archived USDA extract. Its reproduction workflow uses an archived intermediate dataset of qualifying compound-event days rather than reconstructing those days independently from raw daily climate data. The results describe annual yield trajectories and accumulated shortfalls under repeated exposure; they do not establish physiological recovery of the same maize crop. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23279840

title: Key Projects and Design Strategies in Energy-Efficient Contemporary Architecture
description: The built environment accounts for approximately 39% of global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions and over 36% of final energy consumption worldwide. In response to pressing climate imperatives, contemporary architecture has undergone a paradigm shift from conventional resource-intensive design toward ultra-low-energy, net-zero, and energy-positive building standards. This paper conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of iconic energy-efficient architectural projects utilizing the standardized IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) research framework. By evaluating landmark international case studies—including The Edge (Amsterdam), Powerhouse Brattørkaia (Trondheim), Bullitt Center (Seattle), Pearl River Tower (Guangzhou), and the Bahrain World Trade Center (Manama)—this study synthesizes the core mechanisms bridging passive architectural strategies (building orientation, high-performance thermal envelopes, natural ventilation) and active technological innovations (Building-Integrated Photovoltaics [BIPV], geothermal energy loops, and IoT-driven smart automation). Quantitative metrics demonstrate that the synergistic implementation of these approaches can achieve operational energy reductions exceeding 70% relative to regional baseline standards, while generating substantial surplus energy. Finally, the study evaluates technical, financial, and policy barriers and proposes actionable frameworks for adapting green building methodologies to hot, arid continental climates such as Central Asia. title: Lithostratigraphic description, bulk elemental and isotopic composition, rock magnetic and grain density data of cores from the HYDRATE 02 Geo Data Well at Kuparuk State Site 7-11-12, Alaska North Slope
description: Abstract We characterized sediments recovered from the Alaska North Slope during the Collaborative Gas Hydrate Research and Development Project led by a consortium of the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC), U.S. Department of Energy (US-DOE), and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). We analyzed core sediments for sedimentological, bulk geochemical, and rock magnetic properties. This project involved well logging, pressure coring, and a long-term production test at the Kuparuk 7-11-12 State well pad within the Prudhoe Bay Unit. Quantitative degassing (controlled depressurization) of a pressure core allows for measurement of the total volume of released gas in a core and characterization of the composition of the gas. All pressure coring was done using the JOGMEC High Pressure/Temperature Corer (HPTC IV). Drilling operations of the HYDRATE 02 Geo Data Well (GDW) well occurred over 42 days between October 9 and November 19, 2022. The well location was located at 70 degrees 19' 1.84032" N and 149 degrees 12' 0.95289" W. The well was drilled to a total measured depth (MD) of 1084 m (3558 ft). Between 365 m (1199 ft) and the bottom of the hole, the well was drilled at an average inclination of 12.9 degrees with a maximum of 19.3 degrees. All depths are reported as measured depth (MD), based on the length of drill pipe from the rig floor, and as total vertical depth below sea surface (TVD ss), after correcting for the inclination. Eleven pressure cores (Cores 1P through 11P) were collected in the D1 sand and the overlying basal E shale between 722.07 m (2369.0 ft) and 755.78 m (2479.6 ft) MD. Thirteen pressure cores (12P through 24P) were recovered in the B1 sand and overlying basal C shale) between 875.69 m (2873.0 ft) and 915.31 m (3003.0 ft) MD. After the majority of the pressure cores were quantitatively degassed, the core sections were split and scanned for various properties; see Collaborative Gas Hydrate R and D Project in Alaska (2026) for core scan results and core images. After scanning, the lithology of each core section was described and subsamples were collected for discrete sample analyses. These subsamples were analyzed via carbon-nitrogen-sulfur elemental and isotopic analysis, X-fluorescence elemental analysis, grain density measurements by gas pycnometry, and multiple rock magnetic techniques (room temperature, low temperature, high temperature). This data set contains results presented in Phillips and others (2026). This data set is organized into six Excel spreadsheet tables: Table 1. Discrete sample summary (Table1-HY02-GDW-discrete-samples.xlsx), Table 2. Visual core descriptions (Table2-visual-core-descriptions.xlsx), Table 3. Magnetic hysteresis (Table3-HY02-GDW-mag-hysteresis.xlsx), Table 4. Backfield remanence curves (Table4-HY02-GDW-backfield.xlsx), Table 5. High temperature magnetic properties (Table5-HY02-GDW-hi-T-mag.xlsx), and Table 6. Low temperature magnetic properties (Table6-HY02-GDW-MPMS.xlsx). Procedure summary Visual core descriptions were performed on the archive half of cores using approaches typical of scientific ocean drilling (Mazullo and Graham, 1988; Marsaglia and Milliken, 2023) and a grain size gauge based on the Wentworth scale (Wentworth, 1922). title: Machine Learning-Based Predictive and Prescriptive Maintenance for Induced Draft Fan in Steam Power Plant
description: The Induced Draft (ID) Fan at the case-study unit has no installed redundancy. If it fails, the unit is derated by up to 50% or tripped by a Master Fuel Trip. Route-based monitoring finds damage late, because early vibration amplitudes sit below the ISO 10816 threshold. We treated this as a DMAIC problem, fishbone analysis and a Cost-Benefit screen ranked an explainable autodetection layer above analyst training and material fixes. The detector is a 135,750-parameter one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) whose layers follow a Digital Signal Processing (DSP) equivalence (convolution as FIR filtering, max-pooling as envelope demodulation, stacked layers as Zoom-FFT), so an engineer can check its decisions against physics. SHAP attributions are mapped to the frequency and cyclic-spectral domains (CS-SHAP). Run-to-failure data could not be obtained from the plant, and MAFAULDA (50 kHz, 97,550 segments) was used as a surrogate for ID Fan fault modes. With a leakage-safe file-level split (1,560 training, 391 test files), accuracy reached 99% and macro-F1 0.99 over six machine conditions, above the 90% Critical-to-Quality target. CS-SHAP energy clustered on the resonance carrier near f ~ 2 kHz around the BPFO and BPFI markers, as DSP theory predicts. The improvement becomes a condition-based SOP with three-tier early warning and a model-drift control plan. By converting the single annual unplanned event into scheduled work, it targets an MTTR reduction from 120 to 72 hours or 40%,against an estimated IDR 5.70 billion per unplanned event and is projected to reduce ID Fan EFOR from 0.29% toward 0%. title: Molecular Dynamics Dataset of NaCl-Containing Ice Ih Using GROMACS: Temperature-Dependent Structural Properties and Ion-Specific Tetrahedral Order (240–273 K)
description: This dataset contains molecular dynamics simulation inputs, trajectories, and structural-analysis data for sodium chloride (NaCl)-containing hexagonal ice (ice Ih) at nominal temperatures of 240, 250, 260, and 273 K. The simulations were performed using GROMACS 2023.3 and the TIP4P/Ice water model. The simulated system contains 2,284 water molecules, 10 Na⁺ ions, and 10 Cl⁻ ions, corresponding to 10 NaCl ion pairs. The final configuration was subjected to steepest-descent energy minimization and NVT equilibration before production simulations of 1 ns at each nominal temperature. The dataset includes simulation structures, topology and ion-parameter files, molecular dynamics input files, production trajectories, energy and log files, and processed structural-analysis results. The analyses cover oxygen–oxygen and ion–oxygen radial distribution functions, ion–oxygen coordination numbers, hydrogen-bond connectivity, molecular tetrahedral-order parameters, mean-square displacement, and spatially resolved tetrahedral order as a function of distance from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Associated analysis scripts are included where available. The dataset supports examination of temperature-dependent structural changes in NaCl-containing ice Ih and comparison of the local structural perturbations associated with Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The results indicate a modest reduction in global structural ordering with increasing temperature, nearly unchanged average hydrogen-bond connectivity, and pronounced ion-specific spatial heterogeneity in tetrahedral order. The simulations represent a fixed-composition, fixed-volume model over 1 ns trajectories. They are intended to characterize local structural organization and short-time molecular response, rather than to establish long-timescale ion redistribution or equilibrium diffusion. The dataset is provided to support transparency, reproducibility, and further analysis of molecular structure and ion-specific effects in saline ice Ih. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23446540

title: National contributions to climate change due to historical emissions of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
description: A complete description of the dataset is given by Jones et al. (2023) . Key information is provided below. Background A dataset describing the global warming response to national emissions CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O from fossil and land use sources during 1851-2024. National CO 2  emissions data are collated from the Global Carbon Project (Andrew and Peters, 2025; Friedlingstein et al., 2025).  National CH 4  and N 2 O emissions data are collated from PRIMAP-hist (HISTTP) (Gütschow et al., 2024). We construct a time series of cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions for each country, gas, and emissions source (fossil or land use). Emissions of CH 4  and N 2 O emissions are related to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions using the Global Warming Potential (GWP*) approach, with best-estimates of the coefficients taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021). Warming in response to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions is estimated using the transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions (TCRE) approach, with best-estimate value of TCRE taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021, Canadell et al., 2021). 'Warming' is specifically the change in global mean surface temperature (GMST). The data files provide emissions, cumulative emissions and the GMST response by country, gas (CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or 3-GHG total) and source (fossil emissions, land use emissions or the total). Data records: overview The data records include three comma separated values (.csv) files as described below. All files are in ‘long’ format with one value provided in the Data column for each combination of the categorical variables Year, Country Name, Country ISO3 code, Gas, and Component columns. Component  specifies fossil emissions, LULUCF emissions or total emissions of the gas. Gas specifies CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or the three-gas total (labelled 3-GHG). Country ISO3 codes are specifically the unique ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes of each country. Data records: specifics Data are provided relative to 2 reference years (denoted ref_year below): 1850 and 1991. 1850 is a mutual first year of data spanning all input datasets. 1991 is relevant because the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was operationalised in 1992. The  Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables. Data are provided from ref_year-20 because these data are required to calculate GWP* for CH 4 . title: Norway spruce shows stronger growth sensitivity and weaker intrinsic water-use efficiency response than Scots pine under increasing water limitation in southern Finland
description: The data supporting this study consist of tree-ring growth, stable carbon isotope, forest inventory, and climate records collected across southern Finland for the period 1990-2022. Tree-ring samples were obtained from six forest sites, including three Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris L.) stands located on mineral soils and three Norway spruce ( Picea abies (L.) Karst) stands located on organic soils representing contrasting local moisture conditions. Annual basal area increment (BAI) was derived from dendrochronological measurements and used as an indicator of radial growth. Carbon isotope discrimination (Δ¹³C) was estimated and measured from d13c from annual tree rings and used to estimate intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE). To place site-level observations within a broader regional context, the tree-ring records were combined with species-specific growth indices (GIs) obtained from the Finnish National Forest Inventory (NFI). The NFI data represent regional growth dynamics across a wider range of sites and soil conditions than those included in the tree-ring network. Climatic drivers of growth and physiological responses were characterized using annual and seasonal climate variables, including vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and summer water balance. These variables were used to quantify atmospheric moisture demand and water availability and to assess their influence on interannual variability in BAI and iWUE. Site-level analyses incorporated local moisture conditions, whereas regional analyses focused on species-specific responses across southern Finland. The final dataset therefore includes annual observations of (i) tree growth expressed as basal area increment and NFI growth indices, (ii) carbon isotope discrimination and derived intrinsic water-use efficiency, (iii) climate variables describing atmospheric demand and water availability, and (iv) site descriptors including species, soil type, and relative moisture conditions. The dataset was designed to evaluate changes in growth and water-use efficiency under increasing water limitation and to compare species-specific responses across spatial scales ranging from individual forest stands to the regional forest inventory network. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23237170

title: Opportunity losses of green hydrogen production globally, benchmarked against the global green hydrogen project pipeline
description: Green hydrogen has been proposed by some as a solution for hard-to-abate emissions. Assessment its enabled emission reductions typically use fossil-fuels as the counterfactual scenario, overlooking trade-offs from using renewable electricity (RE) that could otherwise have greater effects elsewhere. Here, we quantify the opportunity loss (tCO2/MWh) of using RE for green hydrogen globally using a global geospatial model to assess i) the available renewable electricity, ii) the annual green hydrogen production and iii) emissions effects from a range of end-uses, including direct use of RE, industrial electrification, supporting electric vehicles, powering heat pumps and a range of green hydrogen end-uses. Results are assessed globally using i) the International Financial Institution Technical Working Group's mitigation factors for grid-connected renewables, ii) mitigation potentials for green hydrogen end-uses taken from Terlouw, T., Moretti, C., Harpprecht, C.  et al.  Global greenhouse gas emissions mitigation potential of existing and planned hydrogen projects.  Nat Energy   10 , 1503–1515 (2025) and ii) bespoke models for electrified end-use emissions savings.  Global estimates of the renewable electricity availability and green hydrogen production potential under the cost-optimal electrolyser ratio and wind:solar hybridisation are included in Global_Results_H2.csv. , with details of the optimal electrolyser sizing and wind:solar hybridisation for a 1 MW project at each gridcell. Estimates of the mitigation effects and opportunity losses are benchmarked to the global planned green hydrogen project pipeline in IEA_Project_Benchmarking_Full.csv , with data taken from the International Energy Agency's Hydrogen Project Tracker. title: Peach Leaf Damage - Local Field Dataset (Jumilla, Murcia, Spain)
description: This dataset contains 182 annotated leaf-level images of peach (Prunus persica) leaves cropped from 122 photographs taken in a commercial orchard. It is intended for image-based classification of foliar damage and for studying domain shift between curated public datasets and field imagery. The images were acquired in a 2-ha commercial peach orchard located in Jumilla (Murcia, Spain; 38.438931° N, 1.304664° W), under a semi-arid Mediterranean climate. The orchard was established in 2010 with 'Grocivac 2' (IVIA) cultivar trees grafted onto GF677 rootstock, at a 5.5 m × 3 m spacing. Leaves were sampled from many trees distributed over the plot, detached and photographed on site on a squared reference template with a Google Pixel smartphone, in two campaigns: - 2024: 19 photographs containing several leaves each, from which 79 leaves were annotated. - 2025: 103 photographs of one leaf each, taken with a camera module with a 1/1.3" sensor (50 MP, 1.2 µm pixel pitch) and a fixed 24 mm-equivalent f/1.7 lens. Each leaf was segmented with a polygon in CVAT, cropped and set on a black background, giving one labelled image per leaf. Labels were assigned by an agronomic engineer from visible symptoms. Each image belongs to one of four classes reflecting the conditions naturally present at the site during the acquisition period: healthy: 107 images (57 in 2024, 50 in 2025) mechanical_stress: 44 images (13 in 2024, 31 in 2025) abiotic_stress: 24 images (2 in 2024, 22 in 2025) chewing_insect: 7 images (7 in 2024) Two further classes present in public peach datasets (bacterial_spot and mite_presence) were not observed at the study site during sampling, as the campaigns were conducted under late-season conditions with established phytosanitary and biological control management. To preserve ecological validity, no external or simulated samples were introduced. Files: images/<class>/ contains one JPEG per leaf; metadata.csv gives, for each image, its class, campaign (2024 or 2025) and source photograph. Leaves from the same photograph should be kept in the same partition to avoid leakage between training and test data. This dataset was used as the unseen target domain in the associated publication, both for zero-shot evaluation of models trained on public data and for target-domain adaptation experiments. The source code and the exact partitions are available at https://github.com/adricanovas/peach-leaf-classification. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23475740

title: Pilot-scale integrated LCA and C-LCC analysis for sustainable active material selection in sodium-ion batteries
description: The sustainability of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) is strongly influenced by the environmental and economic performance of their active materials, particularly at early development stages. However, comparative assess- ments of multiple synthesis pathways under harmonized pilot-scale conditions remain limited. In this study, three Na0.7MnO2 cathode synthesis routes (solid-state, sol–gel, and hydrothermal) and three biomass-derived hard carbon anode production pathways (walnut shell via thermal treatment, corn straw via hydrothermal processing, and pomelo peel via chemical activation and carbonization) were assessed within a cradle-to-gate framework. Laboratory-scale data were upscaled to a pilot-scale production scenario (100 kg day 1) using a process-based scaling approach. Environmental impacts were quantified using the ReCiPe 2016 midpoint (H) method, while economic performance was evaluated through Commodity Life Cycle Costing (C-LCC) coupled with Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis.,The results reveal that process configuration and energy intensity dominate sustainability performance, outweighing the influence of raw material origin. Among cathode pro- duction routes, the solid-state method showed the lowest global warming potential (7.3 kg CO2 -eq kg 1) and median C-LCC (3.5 € kg 1), whereas the hydrothermal route exhibited significantly higher burdens (211.5 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 124.2 € kg 1). For anode materials, pomelo peel–derived hard carbon presented the most favorable environmental and economic profile (57.6 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 11.2 € kg 1), while corn straw–based production was strongly driven by electricity demand.,These findings identify energy and auxiliary material intensity as key drivers of sustainability and provide guidance for material and process selection in emerging sodium-ion battery technologies. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19568341

title: Plant occurrence documentation and climate exposure across Brazilian phytogeographic domains: data and analysis archive
description: This repository contains the essential data, code and analytical outputs supporting the study of plant occurrence documentation and projected climate exposure across six Brazilian phytogeographic domains: Amazonia, Caatinga, Cerrado, Atlantic Forest, Pampa and Pantanal. The analysis combines GBIF-derived documentation metrics with an operational climate exposure index based on WorldClim projections for 2041–2060 from MIROC6 and MPI-ESM1-2-HR under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. It distinguishes documentary absence from low positive documentation and examines categorical overlap, continuous spatial association and climatic-space coverage. The archive includes: Aggregated documentation metrics and climate indices for 3,397 analytical cells. Results for continuous spatial models fitted to 3,057 positively documented cells. The two original fitted models and their common spatial mesh. All 998 saved bootstrap responses, with diagnostic statistics and numerical audits. Analysis scripts, result tables and Figures 1–8. Source attribution, software-version records, verification scripts and SHA-256 checksums. The categorical spatial comparisons remain approximate. Both primary continuous coefficient intervals include zero, and an extreme-residual discrepancy limits interpretation of the Gaussian response model. These analyses describe accessible occurrence documentation and relative climate exposure; they do not estimate biological absence, ecological vulnerability, causality or ecological niches. Raw GBIF records, original climate rasters, third-party publications and the large fitted-model objects for individual bootstrap replicates are excluded. Reproduction requirements and archive limitations are documented in the README. Author-owned derived data, figures and documentation are distributed under CC BY 4.0; author-written scripts are distributed under the MIT License. Third-party source materials retain their original licences. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23459279

title: Predicting Band Gap of Perovskite Materials for Solar Cell Application Using Machine Learning Regression Trees and Ensemble Models
description: The urgent global demand for clean energy has accelerated the research into perovskite materials, which are highly praised for their exceptional light-absorbing abilities and ease of large-scale fabrication in next-generation solar cells. A perovskite’s ultimate efficiency is decided by its band gap, which controls the wavelengths of light it harvests. Traditional methods for identifying the ideal perovskite combination, such as trial-and-error lab experiments or intensive computational simulations, are incredibly slow and expensive, creating a significant obstacle to materials discovery. To develop a fast, reliable machine learning framework that accurately predicts band gaps for various perovskite compositions without requiring slow, manual testing. To accomplish the work, we collected a comprehensive dataset of known perovskite materials and extracted their core properties to use as features. These features were then used to train and compare several machine learning algorithms, including Fine Tree (FT), Medium Tree (MT), Coarse Tree (CT), and Bagged Trees (BGT) . Among the implemented models, the BGT model outperforms the others, achieving the highest predictive accuracy (R²) of 94.50% and 98.02% on the validation and test sets for bandgap prediction of perovskite solar cell materials, respectively. This research successfully demonstrates that machine learning acts as a powerful screening tool. By bypassing the traditional trial-and-error approach, this framework provides an accelerated, data-driven path to discovering cheaper, more efficient materials for solar energy. title: Processed CMIP6 Earth System Model Carbon–Nitrogen Cycle Data
description: Overview This repository documents the processing workflow used to derive global annual carbon–nitrogen cycle data from original CMIP6 Earth system model (ESM) monthly output. The development of this dataset was motivated by the development of CNit (Carbon–Nitrogen Interactions in Terrestrial ecosystems; see  CNit documentation ;  Tang et al., 2025a ,  2026a ,  2026b ,  2026c ), the coupled carbon–nitrogen cycle model for MAGICC (Model for the Assessment of Greenhouse Gas Induced Climate Change; see  MAGICC repository ;  Meinshausen et al., 2011 ). During the processing and analysis of ESM output, we identified notable mass-conservation issues that prevented the direct calibration of CNit, which strictly conserves carbon and nitrogen mass. Through investigations involving ESM teams and analysis of the model output, we found that these issues are related to the way carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes are reported in ESM output. Based on these findings, we have provided recommendations for future data providers, data users, and different MIPs. Further details are provided in  Tang et al., (2025b)  and the accompanying  community technical report . The processed dataset ( 17 ESMs across the 1pctCO2 series, historical, and SSP scenarios ) can support a range of applications, including calibration and evaluation of simple climate models (SCMs) at both spatially resolved and global-integrated scales, intercomparison of terrestrial carbon–nitrogen cycle states and fluxes across ESMs, analysis of carbon–nitrogen cycle responses across experiments and scenarios, and evaluation of model consistency and mass conservation. The dataset also provides a standardized annual-resolution basis for analysing the variation and temporal evolution of terrestrial carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes across CMIP6 ESMs.   Changelog 2026-10-08 — Initial upload Added README.ipynb : A notebook documenting the background, data processing and correction procedures, and data distribution. Added notebooks.tar.gz and  environment.yml : Source code and the environment file for reproducing the data processing workflow. Added land_area_related.tar.gz : Multiple .pkl files containing ESM-specific grid area, land fraction, and land area data . Added global_annual_data.tar.gz : A single NetCDF file,  CMIP6_ESM_carbon_nitrogen_cycle_outputs_global_annual_processed_by_Gang_Tang.nc , containing global land-integrated annual data for all ESMs and experiments .    Added annual_data.tar.gz : Multiple NetCDF files containing gridded annual data for each model–experiment combination . This file is not provided here because of difficulties uploading the large global gridded annual data to Zenodo. Instead, it is available from Figshare (link: https://doi.org/10.26188/34089963 ). title: Processed data for coastal flood vulnerability assessment in Xiamen, China, under climate change and socioeconomic development
description: This dataset contains processed data supporting an assessment of coastal flood vulnerability in Xiamen, China, under climate change and socioeconomic development. It includes maximum inundation depth, inundation duration, economic and societal loss estimates, vulnerability indicators, and population exposure statistics. The assessment considers tropical cyclone intensities associated with 10-, 100-, and 1000-year return periods for a 2020 baseline and future conditions in 2100 under SSP5-8.5, with population and GDP projections under SSP5. Additional attribution experiments examine the separate and combined effects of climate change and socioeconomic change. The vulnerability outputs include a dynamic vulnerability index incorporating inundation duration and a comparison vulnerability index. The files are primarily provided in XLSX format as static values without active formulas. The accompanying README and Dataset_Guide.xlsx document the directory structure, scenario codes, field units, data sources, population-input variants, and processing notes. A consolidated Regional Data worksheet provides district-level statistics in a consistent tabular structure. This deposit contains processed research outputs. Original FVCOM netCDF files, bathymetry, and mesh connectivity are not included. Geographic coordinates and derived inundation depths are retained. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23434824

description: v2026.10.0 (2026-10-14) This is a regular monthly PUDL data release, primarily motivated by updating the EIA-860M monthly data through August 2026. It also brings in final release 2025 data for the EIA-860, EIA-861, and EIA-923, plus straggler FERC Form 1 filings from 2025. We've also added the new table core_epamats__hourly_emissions brings hourly mercury and hydrogen chloride emissions into PUDL. Thanks to @bsousa22 for this contribution! Finally, we fixed a longstanding bug in the net generation and fuel allocation that silently dropped legitimate data for generators transitioning between proposed / existing / retired status across a multi-year ETL run. Enhancements Added county_id_fips and state_id_fips to the core_eia__entity_plants , out_eia__monthly_generators and out_eia__yearly_generators tables. See PR #5688 . out_eia__yearly_generators_by_ownership now identifies each generator's operator as well as its owners, via new operator_utility_id_eia , operator_utility_id_pudl and operator_utility_name_eia columns, with foreign key checks on the IDs. See issue #5550 and PR #5585 . New Data EPA MATS Created the core_epamats__hourly_emissions table, bringing hourly mercury and hydrogen chloride emissions data from the EPA into PUDL. See issue #5357 and PR #5572 . Thanks to contributor @bsousa22 for bringing in this data! Expanded Data Coverage EIA-860 Added final release data from 2025 for EIA-860 . EIA-923 Added final release data from 2025 for EIA-923 , and monthly release from June 2026. See issue #5594 and PR #5599 . FERC Form 1 Integrated any updates or straggler filings from 2025 for FERC Form 1 . See PR #5668 . Documentation Fixed dbt macro argument documentation in dbt/macros/schema.yml and dbt/tests/data_tests/generic_tests/schema.yml to match dbt 1.12's stricter validation of macro arguments: blocks against their jinja signatures, clearing a long list of spurious dbt parse warnings. Also standardized on the long-form string type name (rather than str ) throughout, since both are accepted by dbt but were used inconsistently. See PR #5593 . New Data Tests & Validations Added unit tests for the ID assignment process that builds core_epa__assn_eia_epacamd_subplant_ids . Fixed several bugs that those tests exposed, including one that could split a physically connected group of generators into separate subplants. Simplified the underlying ID assignment logic to be entirely graph-based. See issue #5675 and PR #5543 . Part of an effort to harmonize the Open Grid Emissions initiative and PUDL. See epic #5439 which is tracking that effort. Added minimum and maximum constraints for plant and Census latitudes and longitudes, to catch impossible locations. See PR #5697 . Bug Fixes & Data Cleaning Made the EIA-930 and FERC-714 hourly demand imputation deterministic. description: This dataset accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Deep Reinforcement Learning in Renewable Microgrid Energy Management.” The dataset provides processed, hourly renewable microgrid data for developing and evaluating a causality-aware, risk-sensitive economic action-selection method (RSE-AS) applied to battery energy storage management with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) reinforcement learning. Dataset contents Training (2017–2020): 35,064 hourly observations. Validation (2021): 8,760 hourly observations. Testing (2022): 8,760 hourly observations. Additional testing (2023): 8,753 hourly observations, ending December 31, 2023, at 16:00 UTC. Out-of-distribution evaluation (2022): Four controlled scenarios comprising a 20% increase in demand, a 30% reduction in photovoltaic generation, a 50% increase in electricity tariffs, and a combined perturbation scenario. The processed files include electricity demand, photovoltaic generation, electricity tariffs, forecast information, uncertainty estimates, and temporal features. To support causal decision-making, the evaluation workflow constructs decision-time observations using lagged load, photovoltaic generation, one-hour-ahead net-load forecasts, and uncertainty estimates. Temporal alignment and forecast-target timestamps were checked during dataset validation. Original data sources Electricity demand: Hourly Electricity Demand Profiles for Each County in the Contiguous United States . DOI: https://doi.org/10.25984/3366592 Solar resource: National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) . DOI: https://doi.org/10.25984/1810289 The processed data are derived from these sources and include research-specific transformations. Both original sources are attributed in the accompanying DATA_SOURCES.md file. Data availability and reuse The archive contains eight processed CSV files, a README, data-source attribution, and licensing information. The research contributions are provided under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license, subject to the rights and attribution information documented in the archive. title: Raw data for the project 'Upcycling Waste Aromatic Polymers as Adsorbents for Atmospheric Water Harvesting'
description: Plastic pollution and water scarcity are two of the most pressing global challenges of the 21 st century. Conventional recycling approaches such as mechanical reprocessing, pyrolysis, and depolymerisation often lead to material degradation, high energy demands, or low-value outputs. We report an innovative approach to upcycle discarded aromatic polymers into hypercrosslinked networks for sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting. Waste aromatic plastics are crosslinked and sulfonated to yield hydrophilic hypercrosslinked polymers that exhibit excellent water sorption capacity, reaching 0.19 g×g -1 at 30% and 0.57 g×g -1 at 90% relative humidity and 25 °C. This work outlines a potential second service life for waste polymers as robust materials for sustainable water production, bridging the dual challenges of plastic waste management and water scarcity. title: Remote Sensing of Leaf Area Index as an Indicator of Ecosystem Resilience to El Niño-Driven Climate Variability in the UK
description: This dataset contains the data and R code supporting the article “Remote Sensing of Leaf Area Index as an Indicator of Ecosystem Resilience to El Niño-Driven Climate Variability in the UK”. The study analyses monthly MODIS leaf area index (LAI) from January 2001 to December 2023 at four UK sites: Cairngorms National Park (montane heath) New Forest (lowland heath-woodland mosaic) Peak District, Dark Peak (upland blanket bog) Thetford Forest (lowland pine plantation) It relates LAI to the NOAA Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) and to local climate. Contents Supplementary Data 1 (ONI_NOAA_CPC_2001_2023.csv): the monthly Oceanic Niño Index from NOAA CPC, January 2001–December 2023, as used in the study. Supplementary Data 2 (LAI_monthly_2001_2023.csv): monthly MODIS MOD15A2H Collection 6.1 LAI for the four sites, with observed and gap-filled values and standardised anomalies. Column definitions are in Supplementary Table S1. Supplementary Data 3 (climate/): the HadUK-Grid district series of monthly mean temperature and precipitation for the four Met Office districts used (Scotland E, England SE and Central S, Midlands, East Anglia), and the monthly North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) index from NOAA CPC. These are the versions used in the analyses, covering 2000–2023. Supplementary Code 1 (01_data_acquisition.R): downloads the MODIS LAI subsets through the ORNL DAAC MODIS/VIIRS Web Service, and the ONI record. Supplementary Code 2 (02_analysis_figures.R): runs the quality filtering, monthly aggregation, gap-filling, anomaly calculation, lagged and seasonal correlations, and the rolling lag-1 autocorrelation (AC1) resilience indicator. It reproduces the main tables, Figures 3–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S2. Supplementary Code 3 (03_revision_analyses.R): runs the analyses added during revision: 95% confidence intervals and power extended-lag (0–12 months), smoothed and seasonal ENSO correlations the local-climate analysis (ONI → NAO → district temperature and precipitation → LAI) AC1 trend tests corrected for overlapping windows (phase-randomised surrogates, moving-block bootstrap, non-overlapping blocks) an observation-threshold analysis and a synthetic-missingness experiment It produces Supplementary Tables S2–S4 and Supplementary Figure S3. Supplementary Tables S1-S4 (xlsx): the data dictionary and the full results of the revision analyses. README : describes the files and the order to run the scripts (Code 1 → Code 2 → Code 3). All analyses were run in R 4.3 using the packages jsonlite, zoo and ggplot2. Data sources MODIS MOD15A2H Collection 6.1 from NASA LP DAAC ( https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD15A2H.061 ), accessed through the ORNL DAAC MODIS/VIIRS Web Service Oceanic Niño Index and NAO index from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center HadUK-Grid regional climate series from the Met Office National Climate Information Centre (Hollis et al., 2019, https://doi.org/10.1002/gdj3.78 ) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23318380

The paper investigates what published hourly load in California actually measures, tests whether hourly load shapes remain structurally stable once grid-battery charging and behind-the-meter solar are accounted for, and evaluates whether a bottom-up forecast built on stable load layers improves upon official long-term hourly benchmarks. Stocks and Per-Unit Shapes: Grid-battery capacity, rooftop PV adoption, BTM storage, EV fleet trajectories, empirical PV capacity factors, and the rooftop-PV meter effect. Rolling-Origin Forecast Archive: Hourly predictions from the retrospective rolling-origin evaluation (the layered structural model, machine learning benchmarks, and California Energy Commission official forecasts) broken down by origin and target horizon, alongside realized targets and out-of-sample error scores. Planning Metrics & Storage Sizing: Annual load layers, macro drivers, peak-demand metrics, and capacity-sizing simulation outputs. Codebase & Execution Logs: Complete Python pipeline covering every processing stage from raw downloads to publication-ready figures, a master orchestration script to run all stages in sequence, and execution logs matching the reported findings. description: This repository consists of scripts and data necessary for readers to understand, replicate, and extend the results in the manuscript "Attributing 2013–2024 drivers of global ammonia emissions using IASI observations: implications under future climate change," which has Drew C Pendergrass as lead author and Drew T. The code, given in the code.zip file, is also available via GitHub and is available under a permissive license for users who would like to adapt the code (especially the decomposition of emissions trends onto predictor variables) for their own purposes. Posterior best estimate ammonia emissions at daily 4°x5° resolution for 2013-2024, produced in this work from a CHEEREIO inversion of IASI data, is provided at NH3_posterior_emis.nc in this repository. title: Replication package for "Decarbonisation in OECD Economies: A Hybrid LOPCOW–IT2F-CoCoSo and CS-ARDL Framework for Strategic Energy Transformation"
description: This chapter develops and applies an integrated hybrid analytical framework that combines uncertainty-aware fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making with cross-sectionally augmented panel econometrics to evaluate decarbonisation performance and the effectiveness of carbon pricing and green finance instruments in OECD economies over 2007–2023. In the strategic ranking stage, the Logarithmic Percentage Change-driven Objective Weighting (LOPCOW) procedure is combined with the Interval Type-2 Fuzzy Combined Compromise Solution (IT2F-CoCoSo) method to produce a composite decarbonisation performance score across six criteria: CO 2 emissions per capita, primary energy intensity, the renewable energy share, the effective carbon price, green bond issuance relative to GDP, and the OECD Environmental Policy Stringency Index. In the econometric stage, a CS-ARDL panel model is estimated for the long-run elasticity of CO 2 emissions intensity with respect to these drivers, with cross-sectional dependence handled through Common Correlated Effects augmentation; because the short time dimension does not allow country-specific estimation, long-run coefficients are pooled across countries and cross-checked with the cross-sectionally augmented distributed lag (CS-DL) estimator. Three principal findings emerge. First, the country ranking is led by the Scandinavian–Alpine cluster and closed by Iceland, Australia and the United States, with Türkiye in a transitional twenty-fifth position. Second, the renewable energy share is the most robust policy-relevant driver of lower emissions intensity (−0.090, p < 0.001), whereas the effective carbon price has a small, negative and marginally significant long-run effect (−0.009, p = 0.067) that remains negative across five robustness specifications; green bond issuance has no detectable effect, consistent with the additionality debate in the green finance literature. Third, carbon-pricing exposure declines steeply down the ranking, and its joint reading with the ranking identifies three decarbonisation profiles—pricing-intensive leaders, established-pricing intermediate performers and structural laggards with weak or absent pricing—each implying a distinct optimal policy mix. The framework constitutes a diagnostic instrument for differentiated national decarbonisation strategies, with direct relevance to the Turkish emissions trading system established under the 2025 Climate Law. title: Replication package for "Embodied Carbon Liability: Value Added, Not Gross Output"
description: This dataset is the replication package for “Embodied Carbon Liability: Value Added, Not Gross Output” (W.-T. Fang, submitted to Ecological Indicators). It reports, for 927 economy–sector pairs in 71 economies in 2023, the carbon price at which the greenhouse gas emissions embodied in a sector’s exports would equal the domestic value added those exports retain (P*), together with the conventional threshold defined against gross exports (P^gross) and a variant that counts only domestically released emissions (P*dom). Because the conventional threshold exceeds the corrected one by exactly the inverse of the domestic value-added share, the file also gives that share (v) and the resulting overstatement factor (1/v) for every pair. Value added and emissions are drawn from one accounting system: the Asian Development Bank multiregional input–output table for 2023 (74-economy edition, July 2025 release) and its environmentally extended air-emissions table (version of 1 August 2025; CO2, CH4, N2O and F-gases weighted by AR5 GWP100). The source tables are not redistributed; they are available from the ADB Key Indicators Database. Contents: data/thresholds_2023.csv: thresholds, value-added shares, embodied emission multipliers and gross exports for each economy–sector pair (variables and units defined in README.md) data/summary_results_2023.json: every summary statistic reported in the paper data/economy_codes.json: ADB economy codes and names code/: Python scripts that extract the tables, compute the indicators, draw the figures and check the manuscript Figure_1.png, Figure_2.png: the published figures at 600 dpi Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT License. title: Reproducibility Data and Computational Workflow for Nuclear Fukui Response and Marcus Inner-Sphere Reorganization
description: This dataset provides the computational data and workflow supporting the study “Nuclear Fukui Functions and Marcus Reorganization: From Vertical Force Response to Diabatic Work.” It contains Gaussian 16 production input and output files, scripts for input generation and numerical analysis, machine-readable path-integration and reorganization-energy data, computational-environment metadata, workflow documentation, file manifests, and SHA-256 integrity checksums. Four adjacent-charge-state systems are included: N₂⁺/N₂, NH₃⁺/NH₃, naphthalene/naphthalene⁻, and cyclooctatetraene/cyclooctatetraene. The deposited calculations support numerical tests of quadrature convergence, path independence of the finite nuclear force-difference work, and the performance and breakdown of the local harmonic nuclear-Fukui/compliance approximation. This revised release explicitly includes the complete 21-point linear NH3 trajectory used in the manuscript, which was present in the production workflow but was inadvertently omitted from the earlier curated public release. The archive contains the 11-, 21-, and 41-point linear NH3 paths, the 21-point bowed NH3 path, and 21-point linear paths for N2, naphthalene, and cyclooctatetraene. The release contains 330 Gaussian production output files, all with normal termination. It additionally includes four normally terminated Stable=Opt calculations for the open-shell equilibrium states and the structural, vibrational, spin-contamination, and COT soft-mode diagnostics added during revision. Failed or restarted calculations, development-only paths, redundant intermediate data, and Gaussian binary or formatted checkpoint files (.chk/.fchk) are intentionally excluded. Checkpoint-derived formatted files required by the analysis workflow can be regenerated by rerunning the deposited Gaussian inputs and using Gaussian formchk. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23483839

title: Research Dataset and Bibliometric Analysis Outputs for Digital Technologies and Climate Change Education (2006–2026)
description: Overview This repository contains the research dataset, bibliometric analysis outputs, and visualization files supporting the study entitled “Digital Technologies for Climate Change Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Emerging Trends and Research Directions.” The study maps the development of research on digital technologies and climate change education using publications retrieved from the Scopus database. Data Collection and Selection The bibliographic records were retrieved from Scopus on 18 August 2026 using a search strategy combining terms related to climate change education, climate literacy, and digital technologies. The search covered publications from 2006 to 2026. Following the screening and eligibility assessment, 323 documents were retained for the bibliometric analysis. Repository Contents The repository includes the following research materials: Scopus bibliographic metadata: Exported publication records used as the primary dataset for bibliometric analysis, including available titles, authors, abstracts, publication years, source titles, keywords, affiliations, citation information, and references. Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny outputs: Results supporting the analysis of annual scientific production, leading publication sources, influential contributors, thematic structure, thematic maps, and research trends. VOSviewer outputs: Network visualizations used to examine author co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence patterns. Figures and visualization files: Image files corresponding to the figures presented in the manuscript, including the study selection flowchart, publication growth, leading sources, author collaboration network, keyword co-occurrence network, thematic map, and trend topics. Supporting documentation: Available search strategies, data-processing notes, and analysis settings to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. Analytical Approach Bibliometric performance analysis and science-mapping techniques were used to investigate publication growth, influential authors, institutions, countries, and publication sources; scientific collaboration networks; keyword co-occurrence; thematic structure; and temporal research trends. The results were interpreted to identify relationships among digital technologies, pedagogical approaches, and educational objectives in climate change education. Research Purpose and Reproducibility These materials are provided to support research transparency, verification of reported findings, and further investigation of digital technologies in climate change education. Researchers may use the metadata and analysis outputs to explore publication patterns, collaboration structures, thematic relationships, and potential research directions, subject to the applicable data license and the terms of the original data sources. Data Limitations The dataset reflects the Scopus search strategy, indexing coverage, eligibility criteria, and retrieval date. It should not be interpreted as a complete representation of all research on digital technologies and climate change education. Because the search was conducted on 18 August 2026, coverage of publications from 2026 is incomplete. The original Scopus export and analysis settings should be consulted when reproducing the results. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23540960

title: Research data and computational models for Particle delivery and contact-induced interlayer damage in confined graphite processing
description: This dataset supports “Particle delivery and contact-induced interlayer damage in confined graphite processing” by Wenli Zhu, Jiann-Wen Woody Ju and Aihua Zhang. It contains processed experimental input tables, thermal-control data, gas–particle transport event arrays and selected histories, contact-initiation exports, model configurations, executable analysis code and numerical plotting sources. The first-arrival arrays permit independent recomputation of arrival mass, kinetic energy, energy per arriving mass, and the contributions of shared and condition-specific particle identities. The contact data resolve initiation mode under the specified support geometry and interface parameters. These are conditional transport and damage-initiation calculations, rather than predictions of exfoliation yield or complete product distributions. Start with README_PUBLIC.md and the R11 figure/data map. Model definitions, compact solved-array projections and processed exports are identified separately; build-only COMSOL files do not contain saved solutions. Complete large evolution histories are not included in this compact release. Commercial COMSOL and MATLAB licences are required separately to execute the corresponding native models; event-array analysis can be performed with the supplied Python workflow. Author-owned data and documentation are provided under CC BY 4.0; author-owned code is provided under the MIT licence, with third-party notices retained. Microscopy and apparatus images whose redistribution rights are not established, private manuscript files and reference-paper full texts are excluded. Published shared endpoints retain source attribution and do not represent independent replication. Dataset contact: zhuwenli@ucla.edu. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241974

title: Resource efficiency and cleaner production outcomes of digital textile printing with AI-assisted design: a primary field investigation at three Indian commercial facilities
description: This dataset contains interview records and a data-evaluation workbook from a field investigation of AI-assisted digital textile printing at three commercial facilities in Mumbai, India, coded DP-F1, DP-F2 and DP-F3. The facilities were visited on 10, 16 and 24 February 2026. How the data were collected At each facility, the lead investigator conducted a structured interview with a senior member of the design staff during an on-site visit. All values are as reported by facility staff; none were independently measured or metered by the investigators. The records were compiled from the interview notes in March 2026. Contents - Facility Interview Records for DP-F1, DP-F2 and DP-F3, each as PDF and Word. Each covers facility background, process parameters, water and effluent, chemicals and energy, design process and AI tools, and the investigator's qualitative notes. - DP_Data_Evaluation_v2.xlsx: the same values in tabular form, cross-facility summaries, a comparison with the three-facility cohort (R1–R3) of the related manuscript, charts, and a Change Log listing every correction from version 1. - DP_Data_Evaluation_v2_Word_version.docx: a read-only Word copy of the workbook's sheets. Relation to the related manuscript DP-F1 to DP-F3 are a separate cohort from facilities R1–R3 analysed in the related manuscript (Singh, Singh and Abhishek, under review). R1–R3 values appear in the workbook only for comparison. Limitations Values are facility-reported. Screen-print comparison values are averages from three screen-print facilities interviewed in the same investigation; their records are not included here. The process steps covered by each energy figure were not recorded, and the two cohorts' energy figures differ by about an order of magnitude. At all three facilities, reported monthly wastewater exceeds water use per metre multiplied by monthly output; the two figures are not reconciled. Pre-press file-preparation time and wash fastness were not recorded for this cohort. This is an operational dataset, not an ISO 14040/14044 life-cycle assessment. Privacy Facility and personal names are withheld. Version 2 (October 2026) Corrections from version 1 (October 2026): no value reported by a facility was changed. The data are now described as facility-reported interview values rather than "directly measured" meter readings. Facility and staff names are withheld, and individual records no longer contain cross-facility averages. Unsourced benchmarks are removed, and items that were not recorded (wash fastness, pre-press time, ΔE formula) are marked as such. A lead-time conversion (6.5 days = 156 hours) and two units are corrected. The full list is in the workbook's "Change Log" sheet. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23372016

title: RhECAST project
description: This repository is periodically updated . The RhECAST - Rural landscape hEritage and CArbon sequeSTration (HORIZON-MSCA-2022-PF-01)  addresses the urgent need for sustainable land use strategies in the face of the global climate emergency. Supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions programme, RhECAST focuses on agroforestry, a time-honored practice in European countries known for its rural benefits and potential for carbon sequestration. The project specifically targets the Po-Venetian Plain in Italy, a region facing significant atmospheric pollution, and combines landscape archaeology, computer-based modelling, and archaeological soil geochemistry to explore the long-term CO2 sequestration of historical agroforestry practices. RhECAST's innovative approach offers insights into sustainable landscape management and climate change mitigation, with the potential for replication in similar European regions such as Germany, Spain, and Portugal. Through this repository, we provide the data, publications, methods, and models used in RhECAST, fostering further research and application in the field of sustainable land use and carbon sequestration.  Overview This dataset is part of the RhECAST project, focusing on sustainable land use strategies, agroforestry, and computer-based modelling to tackle climate change. It includes geospatial data and Python scripts for processing and analysis. RhECAST_EPPA6.zip : The scripts in this zip. file process GTAP 11 economic data, calibrate inputs for silvoarable technologies in the EPPA6 modelling framework, and analyse model outputs across alternative climate policy scenarios, forestry safeguards and subsidy levels. They support the extraction, processing and visualisation of silvoarable deployment, land use changes, economic indicators and CO₂ emissions and removals between 2020 and 2050. This .zip file includes GDX output datasets for low, medium and high subsidy scenarios. RhECAST_2.0.zip :  This .zip file contains the latest version of the carbon sequestration model based on historical LULC changes between 1929 - 2024 in the Po-Venetian Plain (Northern Italy). ISTAT_Catasto_Agrario_1929.zip : This ZIP file contains all the PDF scans of the Catasto Agrario 1929 by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT). title: SEA historical rainfall dataset
description: Here we present a historical monthly rainfall dataset for Malaysia, Singapore and Sumatra, recovered from colonial government and plantation records and spanning 1875 to 1958. The dataset comprises 14,549 station-year records from 672 weather stations and rain-gauges, each reporting rainfall (in inches) for the twelve calendar months together with a source-printed annual total. Station records have been homogenised and adjusted to remove non-climatic breaks if required, all modifications, recomputed totals are retained with explanatory flags. Every station carries geolocation attributes latitude, longitude, distance to coast and elevation and resolves to one of sixteen administrative regions, from which per-region and national composites are built. The dataset offers an opportunity to understand long-term rainfall variability, flood and droughts, water-resource planning, and the benchmarking of gridded and reanalysis precipitation products over the data-sparse tropics. description: This study aims to develop an IoT-based smart power monitoring system for CCTV to enhance energy efficiency and security. Leveraging the Scrum framework ensured effective project management and team collaboration. The proposed model integrates the ARIMA (Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average) algorithm, demonstrating high accuracy in forecasting energy consumption and costs, validated by low Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) values. The dataset for ARIMA modeling comprises 13 columns and 51,062 records sourced from the history of the implemented SPM application. The three-tier application enhances system adaptability and scalability, providing a responsive user interface for real-time monitoring and data analysis. title: Sea surface Dimethylsulfide Concentration and Emission Flux over the North Atlantic Ocean
description: The dataset represents gridded monthly time series of seawater dimethylsulfide (DMS) concentration and total cumulative sea-to-air emission fluxes over the North Atlantic at a spatial resolution of 0.25°×0.25°. The seawater DMS data were generated using a Gaussian process regression (GPR) model to predict daily concentrations across the North Atlantic Ocean. The predictors used are: CHL, MLD, NO₃, PAR, SSS, Si and SST. The daily sea-to-air DMS flux was calculated using gas transfer velocity (Blomquist et al., 2017) and DMS derived from GPR predictions. The monthly total cumulative emission fluxes (EDMS) were computed by integrating the daily sea-to-air DMS flux over the area of each pixel within the domain and over the days of the month. Further information can be found in the following references: Mansour K., Decesari S., Ceburnis D., Ovadnevaite J. and Rinaldi M. (2023). title: Social Cognitive and Planned Behaviour Model of Indonesian and Indian Pre-Service Science Teachers' Intentions to Teach Climate Change Education: A PLS-SEM Analysis
description: This study examined the factors associated with Indonesian and Indian pre-service science teachers’ (PSTs’) intentions to teach climate change education (CCE) using an integrated model informed by Social Cognitive Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 302 PSTs from Indonesia (n = 208) and India (n = 94). Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) to evaluate direct and indirect relationships. Seven of the nine hypothesised direct relationships were statistically significant. Knowledge was positively associated with self-efficacy and attitude, while emotions were positively associated with attitude but not significantly associated with self-efficacy. University support was positively associated with self-efficacy but not significantly associated with attitude. Both self-efficacy and attitude were positively associated with intention to teach CCE. Indirect effects further indicated that university support was associated with teaching intention through self-efficacy, while emotions were indirectly associated with intention through attitude. These findings suggest that teacher education programmes should complement climate change knowledge with opportunities to strengthen PSTs’ teaching self-efficacy and foster positive attitudes towards CCE. Universities could support these efforts through relevant coursework, practical teaching experiences, and access to instructional resources that prepare future science teachers to integrate climate change into their teaching. title: Souveraineté énergétique et transition écologique : une analyse comparée des stratégies de décarbonation du Maroc et de l'Afrique du Sud
description: Le continent africain conjugue un potentiel renouvelable considérable et un déficit d'accès à l'électricité qui touche près de 600 millions de personnes (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2022). Cet article propose une analyse qualitative, documentaire et comparative des stratégies de décarbonation du Maroc et de l'Afrique du Sud, deux cas retenus pour leurs héritages énergétiques contrastés : diversification tournée vers le gaz et les renouvelables au Maroc, dépendance historique au charbon en Afrique du Sud. Le cadre théorique croise la courbe environnementale de Kuznets, l'identité de Kaya et le Trilemme énergétique, articulés au sein d'une grille comparative à quatre dimensions souveraineté, décarbonation, gouvernance, justice sociale construite à partir d'un corpus de sources institutionnelles et académiques publiées entre 2013 et 2024. Les résultats montrent que les deux trajectoires, bien que difficilement comparables terme à terme, se heurtent à des obstacles structurels proches : financement vert, gouvernance locale, capital humain. Ils confirment aussi que la souveraineté énergétique ne constitue pas, en soi, un frein à la transition écologique. L'article propose enfin, à titre prospectif, un modèle de décarbonation souveraine appuyé sur l'intégration énergétique régionale via la Zone de libre-échange continentale africaine (ZLECAF). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23402462

Microrefugia represent locations where fine-scale topographic, hydrologic, ecological, or disturbance-related conditions may locally buffer ecosystems from regional climate change. The resulting spatial prioritizations are intended to support climate-informed land stewardship and protected-area planning. They can be used to identify areas with high potential to support biodiversity persistence under climate change, evaluate existing conservation networks, and distinguish areas where conservation versus restoration may be appropriate. Analyses were conducted at 1-km spatial resolution in the NAD 1983 BC Albers projection. Ranked Zonation priorities range from 0 (lowest priority) to 1 (highest priority). Climate-type macrorefugia were represented by forward and backward climate velocity for an ensemble of eight CMIP6 global climate models under SSP2-4.5. Climate-velocity values were transformed so that higher values represented greater refugia potential. Species-specific macrorefugia represented areas with relatively high potential to retain suitable climatic habitat through time. Separate Zonation scenarios were developed for: rare species in British Columbia (833 Red-listed, Blue-listed, and SARA Schedule 1 species), grouped by major taxonomic group; 142 climate-sensitive bird species; and 10 dominant tree species in British Columbia. Microrefugia A separate CAZ scenario combined six indicators of microrefugia: topodiversity; cool slopes, glaciers, and wetlands; topographically mediated fire refugia; thermal refugia; drought refugia; and old-growth forest. Inputs were transformed to a common interpretation in which higher values indicated greater microrefugia potential. Binary indicators were assigned values of 0 or 1, while continuous or categorical products were rescaled or reclassified as described in Table 1.  The six microrefugia indicators were equally weighted in the CAZ analysis. Microrefugia were treated as temporally static and therefore used for both future periods. 3. title: Supporting information for "Global and regional Pleistocene benthic δ18O stacks on age models with and without astronomical tuning"
description: Note: The BIGSTACKs are in the file "Zhou et al_Supplementary_data_files.xlsx". Constructing accurate age models for Pleistocene marine sediments is crucial for our understanding of glacial-interglacial cycles and other climatic processes. Benthic foraminiferal δ 18 O stacks, a proxy for ice sheet and climate evolution, are often used for stratigraphic alignment and chronology development in deep-sea sedimentary records, in combination with biostratigraphy, paleomagnetism, and radioisotopic constraints. Selection of an appropriate benthic δ 18 O alignment target influences the derived chronology at a given site, and divergent regional trends in benthic δ 18 O highlight the need for ocean-specific benthic δ 18 O stacks. The specific scientific question to be addressed by a study may also influence whether the alignment target should include astronomical tuning. Here, we introduce three benthic δ 18 O stacks – Atlantic, Pacific, and global – with three distinct chronologies for the global stack that incorporate astronomical forcing constraints to various degrees. The new global stack utilizes data from 224 cores and includes 50% more data than the previous “ProbStack” (Ahn et al., 2017). Hand-tuned regional and global stacks, intended as updates to the “LR04” stack (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005), incorporate chronologies transferred from absolutely dated archives during 0-654 thousand years ago (ka) and an astronomically forced ice sheet model during 654-2700 ka. Due to the heterogeneous nature of the age constraints used for these stacks, we call them BIGSTACK mixed , BIGSTACK mixedA , and BIGSTACK mixedP . For applications where astronomical tuning should be minimized, we present a global stack primarily constrained by geomagnetic reversal age estimates, BIGSTACK magrev . We also develop a third age model, BIGSTACK auto , which uses an automated optimization algorithm to “minimally tune” the stack to the pervasive ~41 kyr obliquity cycle, while avoiding assumptions about astronomical phase relationships. This suite of stacks offers flexibility in choosing δ 18 O stratigraphic alignment targets, to allow a wide range of applications in paleoceanographic hypothesis testing. Feb. 10th, 2026 update : the gap of NaN values in BIGSTACK mixed should be 645-650 ka, but in the previous version was 10 kyrs longer (635-650 ka) by mistake. The reason for a gap in the stack during that period is still valid — it's where two portions of the stack, based on absolutely dated targets (0-650ka) and astronomically tuned ice volume modeling (>650 ka), are joined together. Oct. 7th, 2026 update : we present a new version of BIGSTACK magrev that updates the age of the Brunhes/Matuyama boundary to 773 ka (Suganuma et al., 2018; Singer et al., 2019). We thank Prof. Brad Singer for bringing to our attention the evidence pointing to 773 ka as the boundary age. Other BIGSTACKs remain the same as the last version. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23220134

title: Sustainability in Architectural Design and Urban Planning: A Systematic Review of Strategies for Resilient and Low-Carbon Built Environments, 2013–2025
description: Background : Architectural design and urban planning are strategic fields for addressing the climate and sustainability crises. Design decisions influence building orientation, envelope performance, passive heating and cooling, daylighting, thermal comfort, material selection, and energy demand. Methods: A systematic review and bibliometric analysis of Scopus and Web of Science publications were conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Of the 5349 records identified, 146 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were analyzed using Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and Microsoft Excel. Results: The synthesis of the 146 included studies identified three research themes: (i) decarbonization and energy efficiency through building information modeling (BIM), simulation, and life cycle assessment; (ii) thermal comfort and climate adaptation through passive strategies and nature-based solutions; and (iii) social and economic sustainability linked to urban governance. The bibliometric analysis and co-occurrence maps highlighted the importance of sustainability, energy performance, carbon emissions, and built environment simulation, revealing a convergence of technological, environmental, and planning approaches. Conclusions: The synthesized evidence indicated that progress toward resilient and low-carbon built environments required integrating architectural design and urban planning decisions rather than addressing energy efficiency, decarbonization, and climate adaptation separately. Digital tools and environmental assessment methods supported decision-making, but their usefulness depended on integration with bioclimatic design, passive strategies, green infrastructure, and governance. Given the heterogeneity of the studies, the transferability of strategies should be interpreted in relation to climatic conditions, intervention scale, and urban context. THE CIVIL LAW REGIME OF GREEN ENERGY
description: This article examines the civil law regime of green energy as the set of private-law relations that arise around the generation, sale, consumption and certification of energy from renewable sources. It argues that “green energy” is not a single object of civil rights but a bundle of at least four legally distinct objects: energy (or capacity) as a commodity; the generating installation; the right to the site and to the natural flows (sunlight, wind, water) on which generation depends; and the “green attribute” embodied in guarantees of origin and renewable energy certificates. Using doctrinal, comparative and systemic methods, the article analyses the Civil Code of Uzbekistan, the 2019 Law on the Use of Renewable Energy Sources, the 2024 Law on Electricity, the Law on Public-Private Partnership and the relevant European Union directives. It identifies gaps concerning the legal nature of green attributes, the status of prosumers and energy communities, the allocation of curtailment risk in power purchase agreements, and limited real rights over generation sites, and formulates proposals for their elimination.
