title: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF USING ENGINEERED BIOCHAR IN THE RECLAMATION OF SALINE SOILS FOR CARBON SEQUESTRATION AND THE REDUCTION OF GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS
description: Soil salinization is a major environmental and agricultural challenge that reduces soil productivity, disrupts nutrient cycling, and limits the sustainable use of land resources. Engineered biochar has emerged as a promising soil amendment for saline soil reclamation because of its porous structure, carbon-rich composition, and capacity to influence soil physical, chemical, and biological properties. This article examines the role of engineered biochar in enhancing soil organic carbon storage and mitigating greenhouse gas emissions during saline soil reclamation. Particular attention is paid to biochar production conditions, feedstock selection, salinity and sodicity management, carbon persistence, soil respiration, and nitrous oxide and methane fluxes. The article also discusses the importance of life-cycle assessment, field-scale validation, and context-specific application strategies. It argues that the climate benefits of engineered biochar depend on its stability, production technology, application rate, soil characteristics, irrigation regime, and potential effects on greenhouse gas fluxes. Integrating engineered biochar into saline soil reclamation may support soil restoration and climate-change mitigation when supported by appropriate agronomic practices and rigorous carbon accounting. title: TOURISM IN THE NAVOI REGION FROM A PHYSICAL-GEOGRAPHICAL PERSPECTIVE
description: The Navoi Region of Uzbekistan possesses significant tourism potential determined by its distinctive physical-geographical characteristics, including extensive desert landscapes, geological formations, mountain systems, natural water bodies, unique ecosystems, and a continental climate. The region occupies an important position in the central part of Uzbekistan and includes the Kyzylkum Desert, the Nuratau Mountains, the Zarafshan River valley, and several areas of ecological and landscape significance. These natural conditions create opportunities for the development of ecological, recreational, adventure, geological, landscape, and nature-based tourism. This review examines the principal physical-geographical factors influencing tourism development in the Navoi Region, with particular attention to relief, climate, hydrology, landscapes, biodiversity, and the spatial distribution of natural recreational resources. The study demonstrates that a geographical approach to tourism planning can contribute to the rational use of natural resources, diversification of tourist routes, and sustainable development of tourism in the region. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability. Experimental design and simulations The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026. The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions: Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed S1 Transient Fixed Fixed S2 Transient Transient Fixed S3 Transient Transient Transient S4 Fixed Fixed Transient S5 Transient Fixed Transient S6 Fixed Transient Transient Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers. Changes introduced in GCB2026 In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses. For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover. title: Table_S1_functional_traits_DEPOSIT
description: The home gardens of the Baixada Fluminense (Rio de Janeiro) hold a food heritage under growing pressure. In 14 home gardens, the composition of agrobiodiversity in childhood and at present was reconstructed through interviews, and its support for pollination and its resilience to drought and heat were assessed, taking the ethnotaxon as the unit and the weighted presence of species (WP) as the measure of representativeness. Richness in each home garden remained stable, but the aggregate repertoire shrank selectively, through three processes. In crops, the erosion of ethnotaxa was direct, without replacement (βSNE 0.18 against βSIM 0.11), as in the Fabaceae. It also occurred through a reduction in the frequency of use of species, captured by the gradient component of Bray-Curtis (0.28 of 0.30), as in roots and tubers. In fruit trees, the substitution of native species, adapted to the local climate, by exotic ones prevailed (βBC 0.49 against 0.31). Only Underutilized Food Plants (UFP) preserved floral supply, the architecture of the interaction networks with bees and climatic resilience, an anchor and basis for climate-adaptation solutions. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23319316

title: TbCu7 Stability Screen: validation of public DFT databases against observed metastable phases in Sm–Fe–M alloys (stability proxy table)
description: This dataset tests whether public density-functional-theory (DFT) databases can guide composition selection for metastable magnet phases. It compares energy above the convex hull and computed Fe moments from Materials Project, AFLOW, JARVIS-DFT, NOMAD (Alexandria PBE calculations), OQMD and GNoME (628 entries, snapshot 2026-10-13) with 38 published observations of phases formed in Sm–Fe and Sm–Fe–M alloys (M = Co, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Cu, Si, Ga, Al, Mo; none found for Cr, Mn, Hf) after rapid solidification or mechanical milling, 30 of which are scored. Because no database contains the disordered TbCu7 structure, a stability proxy is built from each database's ordered parents (CaCu5, 2:17, 3:29, ThMn12); the proxy and per-family best entries are given in stability_proxy_table.csv . Main finding: Materials Project, OQMD and Alexandria place no Sm–Fe compound on the convex hull, so their energies for equilibrium Sm2Fe17, metastable TbCu7 SmFe9 and SmFe12 (not formed by melt spinning) differ by less than 5 meV/atom. JARVIS-DFT ranks them correctly but places TbCu7 SmFe9 at 89 meV/atom. AFLOW and GNoME contain no comparable entries. The package contains raw database snapshots with provenance (SHA-256), the curated observation table with DOIs, numbered pipeline scripts (Python), a QA report, four figures and documentation (codebook, limitations, verification checklist). Code: MIT. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0. AI assistance: data retrieval scripts, curation drafting and analysis code were prepared with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic); the author verified the numbers and decisions before release. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23456632

title: The Nonlinear Response of Grassland Soil Inorganic Carbon to Soil Acidification Implies Phase-Specific Carbon Vulnerability
description: Grassland ecosystems represent a major global reservoir of soil inorganic carbon (SIC), a pool whose vulnerability to ongoing soil acidification remains a critical uncertainty for the global carbon cycle. Here, we combined a global synthesis of 2,085 grassland observations with a regional field survey across 23 grassland sites to examine how SIC responds to soil acidification and to identify the factors governing SIC dynamics. We found that the response of SIC to soil pH is fundamentally nonlinear, consistent with carbonate buffering, which explains pH-dependent shifts in carbonate equilibria and SIC sensitivity. Across three predefined pH regimes in grassland soils (alkaline: pH > 7.5; near-neutral: 6.5–7.5; acidic: pH < 6.5), SIC exhibits contrasting pH sensitivities, with steep declines in alkaline soils, transitional responses in near-neutral soils, and low, relatively stable SIC pools in acidic soils. Crucially, the dominant controls on SIC shift systematically across these phases, transitioning from pH-driven carbonate regulation in alkaline soils, to plant-related controls in the near-neutral phase, and to soil texture-mediated stabilization in acidic soils. This phase-dependent framework helps reconcile contrasting reports regarding the relative importance of biotic and abiotic controls on SIC dynamics. During the alkaline-to-near-neutral transition, SIC exhibited the strongest sensitivity to soil pH, suggesting that historically carbonate-rich grasslands may represent potential hotspots of SIC vulnerability under ongoing soil acidification. These findings provide a mechanistic, pH‑dependent framework that improves the prediction of soil carbon‑climate feedbacks and guides strategies to preserve this critical carbon pool. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23363861

title: Transport cancellation and entrance heat sensitivity in thermoviscous Couette Poiseuille flow with finite reservoirs: Supporting numerical data and Python code
description: Overview This repository provides supporting numerical data and computational resources associated with the research article entitled "Transport cancellation and entrance heat sensitivity in thermoviscous Couette Poiseuille flow with finite reservoirs" by Hayati TORE. The study investigates transport cancellation and entrance heat transfer sensitivity in steady, laminar, two dimensional Couette Poiseuille flow with temperature dependent viscosity and viscous dissipation. The computational domain consists of a planar channel connected to finite reservoirs. The channel has a height of 0.2 mm and a length of 10 mm, with prescribed lower and upper wall temperatures of 25 and 30 °C, a reference upper wall velocity of 0.90 m/s, and an adverse remote traction difference of approximately 124.50 kPa. The numerical formulation couples finite element discretization of the momentum and continuity equations with a conservative finite volume treatment of the energy equation. The investigation includes diagnostic equation comparisons, global and directional mesh refinement, coupled manufactured solution verification, and comparisons with published constitutive and experimental evidence. Supporting Research Materials The supplementary materials documented in the manuscript comprise two principal components. Supplementary Material S1: Published silicone oil viscosity comparisons, selected experimental shear data extracted from published figures, source attribution, digitization calibration records, and associated comparison scripts. Supplementary Material S2: Numerical result tables, wall heat transfer profiles, manufactured solution verification records, the saved X8Y computational state, and the numerical implementation. The manuscript also documents figures prepared in high resolution PNG and vector PDF and SVG formats. Principal Numerical Findings The finest reported fully coupled calculation uses 95,700 finite volume cells. The dimensionless net transport is −0.01302163, resulting from forward and reverse transport contributions of 0.14354223 and 0.15656386, respectively. Successive streamwise refinement from X4Y to X8Y changes the net transport by 0.076530% and the entrance heat transfer integral by 0.558570%. These comparisons satisfy the selected 1% successive change criterion for the two integral quantities. The manufactured solution tests demonstrate decreasing numerical errors under mesh refinement. The results characterize the prescribed numerical boundary value problem; independent physical validation of the finite reservoir configuration remains incomplete. Reproducibility and Scope The supporting materials document the numerical methods, computational results, and selected comparisons reported in the associated manuscript. Original raw experimental datasets from the cited publications are not included. The author is responsible for the scientific interpretation and reported numerical results. Author Hayati TORE Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Hitit University, Çorum, Türkiye ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1855-9182 DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23392880

title: Turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate estimated by CTD-attached thermistor FP07 onboard R/V Ryofu-maru R/V Keifu-maru on 137E meridian
description: Fast response thermistors FP07 are attached to CTD (conductivity, temperature, and depth profiler) and measure microstructure in temperature. The measurement can be used to estimate turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate. On some of the cruises nominally along 137°E meridian, south of Japan, CTD casts have been made onboard R/V Ryofumaru and R/V Keifumaru , reserch vessels of Japan Meteorological Agency. The CTD data are publicly available from their data site. However, the turbulence kinetic energy dissipation rate is not available on the site and it is posted here. The file is in the CSV format. Two sensors were usually used concurrently, indicated by 'T1' and 'T2' in the first and second columns. Turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rates are in W/kg. The following columns are latitude, longitude, date (year/month/date), temperature, salinity, potential density, and cruise name. The data processing followed the standard method. The references are Y. Goto, I. Yasuda and M. Nagasawa (2018): Comparison of turbulence intensity from CTD-attached and free-fall microstructure profilers. title: Urban Thermal Comfort in Uzbekistan (Termez): Evaluating Microclimate Design and Climate Resilience in Hyper-Arid Public Spaces
description: Hyper-arid urban environments in Southern Uzbekistan, such as Termez, experience extreme summer thermal stress characterized by ambient temperatures exceeding 42°C, elevated direct solar irradiance, and pronounced Urban Heat Island (UHI) effects. This study presents a rigorous microclimatic investigation into outdoor thermal comfort across key public open spaces in Termez using the IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) framework. Utilizing field meteorological measurements, sky-view factor (SVF) evaluations, and ENVI-met numerical simulations, the research assesses the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) and Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) under baseline conditions and three climate-responsive design scenarios: high vegetation canopy density (VCD), high-albedo surface retrofits (albedo ≥ 0.70), and passive shading structures. The baseline results demonstrate extreme heat stress, with peak UTCI values surpassing 44°C and daytime PET exceeding 46°C, severely restricting public social activities and pedestrian stay durations between 11:00 and 17:00. The scenario analyses reveal that integrating a dense tree canopy (VCD ≥ 45%) with high-albedo permeable pavements achieves a peak UTCI reduction of 3.8°C to 5.2°C and lowers mean radiant temperature (Tmrt) by up to 14.5°C in high-exposure plaza typologies. Furthermore, microclimate-responsive spatial design is shown to extend public space usability by 3.5 hours during extreme summer days, strongly correlating with higher social interaction intensity. These findings underscore that urban open spaces in arid Central Asian cities must be planned not merely as passive recreational zones, but as vital climatic infrastructure essential for long-term urban resilience. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23472967

title: Viçosa Urban Microclimate Weather Dataset: EPW Files Based on Local Measurements and Future Climate Scenarios
description: This repository contains a collection of weather files in EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) format developed to represent the urban microclimatic variability of Viçosa, Minas Gerais, Brazil, as well as future climate projections. A key characteristic of the baseline files is that they are stitched (synthetic) annual weather series (8,760 hours) created by integrating hourly regional meteorological data from the National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) with high-resolution, local microclimatic measurements of air temperature and relative humidity. Local measurements were obtained across 16 strategic urban points using automated Onset HOBO thermo-hygrometers during three seasonal field campaigns (Winter 2025, Spring 2025, and Summer 2026). For hours outside these specific field campaigns, reference data from the INMET station were retained to complete the full annual cycle. title: Wasted Light Ledger: VIIRS Brightness Allocated to Published U.S. Wasted-Light Totals for Designated-Place Counties and Communities (2026-10-24)
description: Dataset behind the Wasted Light Ledger (https://darksky-ledger.straitresearch.org), part of the Strait Research Dark-Sky Advocacy Suite. For every U.S. county hosting at least one designated dark-sky place (122 of 122 covered) and for 37 of 43 U.S. Designated Communities with a documented Census place basis, the tool computes an upward-flux proxy from the VIIRS nighttime-lights grid (mean 0.1-degree cell radiance over the jurisdiction, x Census land area) for 2012 and 2024, and allocates the PUBLISHED national wasted-outdoor-light totals of DarkSky International ($3.3 billion/yr; 21 million tons CO2/yr, retrieved 2026-10-24, no reference year stated by the publisher) in proportion to that proxy. Allocated dollar and CO2 figures are ESTIMATEs under stated assumptions (uniform waste fraction; proportionality between the radiance proxy and wasted energy; national totals as published) - the full method, factors with citations, and exclusion reasons are in the methods file. Jurisdiction basis: U.S. Census Bureau Geocoder (Census2020 vintage) for point-to-county resolution; Census Bureau TIGERweb Census2020 layers for land area (AREALAND) and 2020 population (POP100); 2024 Gazetteer files for community name matching. Brightness source: Annual time series of global VIIRS nighttime lights 2000-2024 at 500 m (OpenGeoHub, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17294744, built on Annual VNL V2, Elvidge et al. 2021), sampled with the suite's shared grid sampler; designated places from the Designated Places Registry (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23625002). title: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers
description: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop ( Δ P), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 M Ω ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23348943

title: When Rivers Become Bottlenecks: A Transmission-Based View of Supply Chain Resilience Under Recurrent Climate-Related Transport Constraints — Replication Package
description: Replication package for a recurrent-event study of supply chain resilience under climate-related transport constraints in the Brazilian Amazon. The package combines official hydrological benchmarks from SGB and ANA, industrial indicators from SUFRAMA, and monthly Manaus foreign-trade data from MDIC/Comex Stat. It contains source extracts, cleaned analysis files, an SH4-to-subsector crosswalk, executable Python code, robustness outputs, and validation logs. The workflow separates hydrological extremity, realized inbound disruption, and downstream industrial consequence. The package reproduces all six downstream transmission models, exact small-cluster Rademacher inference, critical-window robustness, and leave-one-subsector-out sensitivity. The empirical record shows that the 2024 low-water episode was hydrologically more extreme than 2023 while realized critical-window inbound flows were substantially stronger; robust pre-critical retiming was concentrated in five high-confidence SH4 families, and downstream revenue models did not show a stable positive pass-through under exact small-cluster inference. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23376125

description: This replication package contains the analytical data, R code, intermediate outputs, robustness diagnostics, figures, and documentation supporting the study “When Twin Transitions Compete: AI Acceleration, Digital Absorptive Capacity, and Renewable-Capacity Expansion in the European Union.” The study examines the EU-27 over 2015–2025 and evaluates whether economies with greater predetermined digital absorptive capacity experienced different renewable-capacity trajectories during the post-2022 acceleration in artificial intelligence. title: Who pays for LNG-based gas expansion? Tariff design, anchor margins and cost recovery in Ecuador
description: Ecuador has moved gasoline and diesel close to import parity but still subsidises household LPG and sells fuel oil to public power plants at a regulated price, and any expansion of natural gas would now depend on imported LNG. This paper asks whether a tariff rule could recover the cost of an LNG terminal and distribution networks in Santa Elena province, and who would bear the loss if none could. A 20-year model calibrated to plant energy data separates the utility, the state power company (CELEC), the treasury and Petroecuador, and users; it consolidates the public sector without double counting transfers and compares tariff rules, household support schemes with bill-responsive adoption, dispatch scenarios and fuel-oil price assumptions. With LNG at USD 9.5/MMBtu, utility NPV is −USD 358 million at 12 % and the consolidated public sector loses USD 337 million at 3.77 %. The anchor customer sets the limit: power plants buy fuel oil at USD 0.48/gal, a third of its export value, and would accept at most USD 0.12/m³ for gas that costs USD 0.40/m³ to land. Even at its export value, the fuel oil is worth less than LNG, so a larger anchor enlarges the loss. A cost-of-service tariff triggers a death spiral, while capacity payments, capital grants or a corrected fuel-oil price only move the loss among public entities. Regulators should require an explicit allocation of volume, contract and fuel-price risk before approving LNG-based distribution. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23518169

title: XRF image of MHNM-KK-OT 03a (from the Jbel Oum Tkout Lagerstätte; Upper Cretaceous, 100 Myr, Morocco)
description: XRF spectral image of a newly discovered teleost fish of unknown affinities (MHNM-KK-OT 03a). Synchrotron XRF spectral raster-scanning was performed at the DIFFABS beamline of the SOLEIL synchrotron source (Saint-Aubin, France). XRF maps were collected at an excitation energy of 17.2 keV optimized for excitation of K-lines from phosphorous to yttrium and L-lines from cadmium to lead. The X-ray beam was collimated by 2 bendable mirrors, monochromatized (ΔE/E ~ 10 −4 ) using a Si(111) double-crystal monochromator and focused using a Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror down to a diameter of 10×7 µm 2 (H×V, full width at half maximum). A 500 ms counting time was used to obtain good statistics on trace elements at an energy of 17.2 keV. Photon flux at this energy is 5.10 9 photons/s in the focused spot. The sample was mounted on a xyz scanner stage, allowing ± 12 mm movements with better than 500 nm accuracy. The sample is orientated at 45 to the incident beam and at 45 to the detector for XRF signal collection. The detector used was a photon-counting four elements silicon drift diod detector (SDD) for the newly identified teleost fish (Vortex ME4, total active area: 170 mm 2 ). The SDD is placed at 90 from the incident beam in the horizontal plane (plane of the electron orbit in the synchrotron). Consequently, the isotropically emitted fluorescence is recorded with strongly reduced Thomson scattering (in theory null). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23578869

description: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) are increasing under climate change. The harmful algal blooming dinoflagellate  Protoceratium reticulatum  is a major producer of yessotoxins (YTXs) that can damage biological tissues. While climate change alters multiple environmental conditions, the combined impacts on  P. reticulatum  growth and toxin production remain poorly understood. In this study, we first applied an orthogonal experimental design to determine the effects of environmental factors among temperature, salinity, initial pH value and eutrophication related nutrients. We then conducted a full factorial experiment to examine the interactive effects of the two most essential factors, temperature (ranging from 15 to 27.5 °C) and salinity (ranging from 21 to 33 ppt) on growth (measured as cell density) and intracellular homoyessotoxin (hYTX) content of  P. reticulatum  K-1477. Furthermore, we evaluated how these factors influence the response on two key copepods species,  Acartia tonsa  and  Nitokra spinipes . Our results showed statistically significant interactive effects of temperature and salinity on cell density and intracellular hYTX content. Salinity only caused significant differences at 30 and 33 ppt under 20 and 22.5 °C, suggesting temperature might be the dominant driver of growth and toxin production. No significant relationship between cell density and intracellular hYTX content was found. Finally, exposure assays revealed reduced swimming speed of  A. tonsa  and increased swimming speed of  N. spinipes  after exposure to  P. reticulatum . These findings demonstrate that warming and salinity fluctuations can modulate  P. reticulatum growth and toxicity, underscoring the importance of multi-stressor approaches for predicting harmful algal bloom dynamics under future climate scenarios. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22286950

title: ecoTrace biogas-sensor pilot, Kiambu County, Kenya: sensor telemetry, gas composition, household survey and derivation code
description: Sensor telemetry, reference gas-composition measurements and a de-identified household survey from a household-biogas monitoring pilot on the ABPL digester fleet in Kiambu County, Kenya (2026-01-27 to 2026-07-19), together with the code that derives corrected gas flow and methane composition from the raw device output. Covers 22 devices, 2,975 device-days and 5,499,810 telemetry rows. The deployed firmware crossed the two thermistor ADC channels, so the raw flow and composition columns are corrupted; the included derivation code undoes the channel swap and recomputes both quantities. Release 1.1.0 adds flow_zero_cal, the corrected flow with a per-unit, temperature-dependent zero-flow calibration. It also adds gap_fill_L, the unmeasured gas next to rows with gas in use (sleeps during use, starts and ends of use), filled at the row's own flow. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23414472
